items: The dependence on HF-selected k-points for the phase factors could bias nodal quality and may limit adaptability to strongly correlated metallic systems; the sensitivity of results to this choice is not fully explored.

Cusp conditions (electron-electron and electron-nuclear) are not explicitly enforced; while the envelope terms might help, a more rigorous discussion or ablation would strengthen confidence in all-electron accuracy.
The role and necessity of the specific periodic functions f and g in the metric M (Eq. 2) are not ablated; robustness to these choices is unclear.
Error bars and variances are not consistently reported on all plots; quantifying stochastic uncertainties is critical for a fair comparison with QMC baselines.
Graphene cohesive energy is compared primarily to experiment and Γ-only vs corrected results; direct comparison to high-level QMC (e.g., DMC, AFQMC) would strengthen claims.

For LiH, the empirical HF finite-size correction relies on a Gaussian basis (cc-pVDZ) HF reference, which may not match planewave all-electron accuracy; justification and sensitivity checks are needed.
Limited discussion of scaling, wall-time, and GPU cost relative to established QMC methods; readers need guidance on practicality at larger sizes.

Notation around supercell vs primitive-cell twists and periodicity conditions (Eq. 4) is dense and may confuse readers unfamiliar with many-body boundary conditions; a brief derivation or clearer exposition would help.
Algorithm 1 contains minor typographical issues and some ambiguous variable naming that make it harder to reproduce.
Some figures (e.g., HEG correlation errors) would benefit from direct numeric tables/error bars in the main text, not just in Supplementary.

While recent periodic neural-network studies (e.g., Wilson et al., Cassella et al.) are cited, direct empirical comparisons on overlapping benchmarks are limited; discussion on how the proposed approach differs (e.g., in feature construction, training stability, or accuracy) would be valuable.

Additional coverage of periodic neural ansatz variants (e.g., PauliNet-style Jastrow/backflow hybrids adapted to PBC) and how the present approach relates or could integrate them would contextualize novelty.

Memory and computational scaling with the number of training states: storing all Γabijkl scales as O(N^2 L^4) and may become prohibitive in realistic basis sizes; costs of computing transition 2‑RDMs between many pairs of DMRG/CAS states are not fully quantified.

Dependence on a consistent SAO ordering breaks permutation invariance for identical atoms and may complicate trajectories with atom exchange or symmetry operations; practical strategies to handle reordering are not yet in place.

The approach assumes adiabatic continuity; behavior near strong avoided crossings, conical intersections, or state reordering is not fully analyzed. Multi‑state tracking and nonadiabatic couplings are acknowledged but not demonstrated.
Fixed active spaces (in CAS-based training) may be suboptimal across geometries with changing correlation character; this could limit reliability without adaptive active spaces.

Comparisons to ML force fields use a GAP model not trained on forces and without the strongest modern architectures (e.g., NequIP, MACE, ACE variants with long‑range or charge‑aware extensions), which weakens claims of superiority over ML potentials.

Most demonstrations employ minimal/modest basis sets (STO‑6G, 6‑31G, cc‑pVXZ with small active spaces). Evidence for scalability to larger molecules/basis sets and long (multi‑ps) trajectories is limited.
No quantitative assessment of NVE energy conservation (drift), force continuity, or robustness to integration step size is reported; these are critical for MD credibility.
Complexity and wall‑time profiles for precomputation vs. inference are not provided, leaving practical feasibility under‑specified.
The “provable convergence to near‑exact” phrasing may overstate guarantees; more careful statements about variational bounds and convergence conditions would improve precision.
Force derivations are delegated to the SI; a concise main‑text summary of the key terms (Pulay-like contributions from AO→SAO transformation and subspace response) would help readers assess rigor.
The active-learning distance requires differences of two‑electron integrals; computational overhead and possible low‑rank approximations merit more discussion.

A deeper discussion of connections to non‑orthogonal configuration interaction (NOCI), selected CI with non‑orthogonal bases, and other subspace interpolation/continuation strategies would better situate the contribution.

Recent charge‑aware and long‑range MLIPs, and physics‑grounded latent‑space models (e.g., Atlas/ECT‑EAM) that are also variational in internal variables and explicitly transmit electronic information, deserve consideration as complementary baselines/approaches.

Quantum rate methodology requires more explicit description: how “quantum Bennett–Chandler” is implemented (RPMD dynamics vs PIMD sampling only), choice of dividing surface (centroid vs bead-based), and treatment of thermostats during flux correlation.
Convergence with respect to bead number at low T (273 K) may require >16 beads for proton motion; reported convergence is referenced to SI but would benefit from explicit main-text quantification.
The 36T cell and NVT ensemble could introduce finite-size and thermal-expansion artifacts; cell-size/ensemble-sensitivity checks are not shown.
Isotope effects (H/D KIE) are not reported; these would provide a stringent validation of the NQE treatment and facilitate experimental comparison.
Rate uncertainties for kBC (classical and quantum) are not prominently reported in the main text; error propagation from FES and flux-side statistics could be clearer.
Sensitivity to the choice of collective variable and to supplemental restraints (“wall potentials”) is not quantified; committor tests are not presented.
The description of reactive-flux calculations in the quantum case is terse; readers may not infer whether standard RPMD-rate theory conventions were followed.
The rationale for bead number, timestep, and thermostat parameters, especially across the temperature range, could be more transparent in the main text.

While the preprint predates some literature, contextualization with later MLP zeolite work capturing proton transfer (e.g., broadly transferable SchNet-based zeolite NNPs) would strengthen positioning.
A brief comparison to alternative rate theories for quantum effects (e.g., instanton theory at low T, RPMD/CMD variants) would help scope the approach.
Quadratic scaling in the number of atomic pairs can limit applicability to larger systems; no analysis of computational/memory scaling or accuracy as molecular size grows.
Distance-only supervision requires a separate nonlinear reconstruction that can fail or be sensitive to weighting; details on constraint handling, weighting schemes, and robustness are sparse.
The “bonding threshold” used for analysis (156.6 pm) is element-agnostic and may be chemically inconsistent across atom pairs; covalent radii-based criteria would be more appropriate.
Limited IRC validation (only on high-energy-error cases) leaves ambiguity about how often predicted TSs truly connect the intended reactant/product across the full test set.
No head-to-head downstream comparison: baseline models (TSGen/TSNet) are not evaluated through the same QC saddle-point/IRC pipeline, so end-to-end benefits remain partly inferential.
Ablations are missing for key design choices (use of interpolated structure, PSI vs simpler encoders, multi-task readouts for energy/entropy) to substantiate their contributions.
Potential dataset quality issues are acknowledged, but there is no systematic audit to separate model error from data noise.
Multi-task predictions (energies/entropies) are introduced but not quantitatively evaluated; their role in improving TS distance predictions remains unclear.
Details on the nonlinear optimization objective, weighting of distances (near vs far), and how ensemble predictions are combined in the objective are insufficient.
Runtime claims (e.g., 2000 TS inferences with a 90-model ensemble in ~1 minute) would benefit from precise benchmarking (batch size, GPU utilization, per-sample latency).
Discussion does not consider more recent generative or guidance-based TS methods and OOD generalization strategies. Notably:
ASTRA (score-based diffusion with a priori TS guidance using only metastable state samples) addresses TS discovery without TS-labeled data and emphasizes multi-path generation.
Conformer-based self-supervised pretraining for OOD generalization shows strong gains for unseen elements and catalytic systems, a key limitation for HCNO-trained models.
No experiments probing OOD generalization (e.g., beyond HCNO) or cross-dataset transfer beyond SN2.
Local-only architecture with fixed cutoffs may struggle with long-range interactions (electrostatics, charge transfer) and nonlocal polarization without explicit treatments or larger cutoffs.
Restricting irreps to l ≤ 1 may limit expressivity for highly anisotropic interactions or subtle higher-order angular correlations; the trade-off is not quantified.
Force-only training is used in several benchmarks; energy accuracy and thermodynamic consistency (e.g., relative energies, reaction barriers) are underreported.
Limited analysis of training stability and long-time MD energy conservation (NVE drift, maximum stable timestep); many MD runs use a conservative 0.25 fs timestep without a systematic study.

Comparisons to baselines are strong for the paper’s time of writing, but modern equivariant/local-frame baselines and time/accuracy trade-offs (e.g., Allegro/MACE/Equiformer-like or frame-based methods) are not discussed.
The DeepMD comparison uses drastically different training set sizes; while compelling, it would benefit from matched-train-size baselines and variance across multiple random seeds/splits.
Limited reporting on stress predictions and finite-strain behavior, which matter for materials applications.
Some implementation details are sparse for reproducibility: optimizer/scheduler, batch sizes, loss weights when energies are included, and exact parameter counts per model.
Minor equation formatting artifacts interrupt the flow; a consolidated notation table would help.

The discussion does not connect to emerging alternatives that reduce tensor-product overhead via local frames or learned frame transitions, nor to scalable, strictly local equivariant variants emphasizing throughput; a forward-looking discussion would help readers position NequIP in the evolving MLIP landscape.
Inversion performance remains limited due to coil architecture and element pairing (16Tx driven by 8 RFPA channels), constraining whole-brain uniform T1-weighted imaging.
Only second-order B0 shimming; unclear how higher-order shims or dynamic shimming would further reduce off-resonance and benefit EPI/fMRI.
Inter-field comparisons (3T vs 7T vs 11.7T) use different subjects and do not include quantitative SNR/CNR, tSNR, or g-factor analyses; conclusions on SNR scaling are primarily qualitative.
Safety results are reported as “no significant differences” without effect sizes, confidence intervals, or power/equivalence analyses; potential for Type II error is not addressed.
Lack of quantitative image quality metrics (e.g., flip-angle NRMSE maps per subject, spatially resolved SNR/CNR, laminar contrast line profiles) to substantiate “mesoscale” claims.
Key safety and performance metrics are relegated to “extended data”; the main text would benefit from summarizing statistics (e.g., p-values/CI for vestibular/cognitive, micronuclei rate changes).
Limited detail on SAR margins (peak local/global SAR vs IEC limits, margins consumed during each sequence, thermal modeling assumptions, and monitoring).
Context with prior ultra-high-field human imaging at 9.4T and 10.5T (beyond safety) could be expanded to better position imaging performance and RF strategies.

Limited discussion of alternative non-pTx strategies (e.g., dielectric shimming, multi-spoke universal pulses vs subject-specific pulses, or sequence designs with built-in B1+/Δf0 correction) and their trade-offs at 11.7T.
The fit quality (reduced χ² ≈ 2.0) remains above unity even after including the 3S component, suggesting either underestimation of uncertainties or incomplete modeling of lineshape/systematics.
Heavy reliance on simulation-derived power corrections C(f) and field maps without an experimental cross-check of microwave field amplitudes/phases and their frequency dependence.
Two-level approximation under linearly polarized fields may not fully capture multi-level couplings and residual Zeeman structure in weak stray fields.
Sparse frequency sampling (seven points plus “TL off”) limits robustness of lineshape determination and may increase sensitivity to modeling assumptions and background subtraction.

The 3S “observation” is inferred from fit improvement and amplitude ratios, lacking an independent control knob (e.g., adjustable E-field quench upstream) to modulate only the n = 3 population for verification.
No demonstrated power-scan (Rabi/AC-Stark scaling) to validate the simulation-based power corrections and to bound residual AC-Stark or saturation effects empirically.
Some notational inconsistencies (e.g., mF vs MF) and scattered details on field calibration and background stability make it hard to fully reproduce the systematic estimates.
The correlation between parameters in the composite fit (SBKG, B2S, B3S, foffset) is not reported, hindering assessment of parameter degeneracies.

A more direct discussion of alternative high-precision schemes (e.g., separated-oscillatory-fields/Ramsey for narrowing) and how this measurement informs or transitions to those techniques would strengthen the outlook.
Limited quantitative comparison to prior muonium LS measurements on lineshape systematics (e.g., line pulling from neighboring hyperfine components) beyond statistical improvements.

The chosen relativistic two-body P-wave Breit–Wigner model is an approximate description for a three-body D0D0π+ final state near an S-wave D*D threshold with finite D* width; threshold dynamics and coupled-channel effects are likely important.

Reliance on Wilks’ theorem for significance estimates near kinematic thresholds and under parameter boundaries may not be fully reliable, though the very large observed significance likely renders this a minor issue for discovery claims.

Use of sPlot-based statistical subtraction assumes negligible residual correlations between the discriminating D0 masses and the D0D0π+ mass; while cross-checked with tight mass windows, a quantitative assessment of residual bias would strengthen the claim.

The analysis largely focuses on establishing the signal and determining δmBW, ΓBW, without presenting kinematic differentials (pT, rapidity) or production rates, which could offer early discrimination between molecular and compact scenarios.
Minor notation inconsistencies (e.g., occasional Tcc++ vs Tcc+) and typographical artifacts from PDF extraction; while not detrimental, a thorough pass for consistency would improve readability.
The motivation for the P-wave “two-body” AB construction (with mA = 2mD0 and mB = mπ) would benefit from a clearer justification and discussion of its limitations in the near-threshold regime.

The Letter could more explicitly situate its findings relative to lattice-QCD results on I = 1 DD(*) scattering (no near-threshold poles) and the emerging consensus that Tcc is an I = 0 (1+) state, emphasizing complementarity.
Brief mention of expectations from effective-field-theory and Flatté-like parameterizations near D*D thresholds would better contextualize the chosen lineshape and its limitations.

Assumption of identical mass-shape PDFs for baryon and antibaryon components in simultaneous fits could bias yield asymmetries if small charge-dependent resolution or tail effects persist; while alternatives were tried, explicit asymmetry in shape parameters was not explored.

The reliance on fixed signal-tail parameters from simulation (for some components) can be a source of bias; a more extensive floating of shape parameters or per-subsample calibration would further de-risk the extraction.

The nuisance-asymmetry cancellation hinges on accurate kinematic matching between signal and control; while addressed, residual mismodelling across the four localized phase-space regions could differ from the global case.
The BDT training description does not explicitly demonstrate charge-symmetry of inputs/response; absent that, a small charge-dependent selection efficiency could leak into the raw asymmetry.
Limited discussion of potential Λ0_b polarization differences between baryon and antibaryon (expected small at LHCb, but could interplay with angular acceptance in a four-body final state).

For localized ACP results, it is not fully detailed whether all nuisance-asymmetry corrections and their uncertainties were recomputed in each region (with region-specific kinematics) and how region-to-region correlations were propagated.

Tabulated breakdowns per subsample (year, polarity, trigger category) of raw and corrected asymmetries are referenced but not shown; including them would strengthen transparency and aid external scrutiny.

The selected phase-space regions are motivated by resonance content, but the predefinition procedure and protection against selection-induced trials (beyond the look-elsewhere correction) could be described more explicitly.

The paper situates itself well relative to earlier null results in charmless Λ0_b decays, but could add a brief contrast with the recent evidence for CPV in Λ0_b → J/ψ pπ− vs J/ψ pK− (ΔACP ≈ 4%, ~3.9σ when combined), to contextualize the emerging picture of CPV in baryons across different topologies.

The amplitude relies on isospin symmetry for Tcc+ → D*D couplings; isospin breaking beyond mass/width differences may be non-negligible at the O(100 keV) level near threshold and could bias extracted scattering parameters.

The fit fixes |g| to a large value in the baseline, placing the model in a scaling regime; although lower limits are quoted, some physical quantities (effective range r, compositeness Z) become weakly constrained and model-dependent.
Wilks’ theorem is used for significances and |g| profiling in a regime with parameters near physical boundaries and non-Gaussian likelihoods; this can be optimistic without toy-MC validation.

The background model is largely parametric (phase-space × polynomial). While variants are explored, a purely data-driven cross-check (e.g., mass-sideband or wrong-sign control regions) near threshold would further de-risk shape biases that could mimic cusp-like enhancements.

The abstract mentions an “unexpected dependence of the production rate on track multiplicity,” but no quantitative results or systematics for production observables are provided here (at least in the provided text).
Relative-yield comparisons among D0D0π+, D0D0, D+D0 require careful efficiency corrections across different kinematic/topological selections; details are referenced to Methods but not visible here.

Several key details reside in Methods (e.g., explicit amplitude equations, treatment of second-sheet continuation, mapping to A_NR for scattering parameters), making it difficult to fully assess technical assumptions from the main text alone.
The compositeness Z limit is discussed qualitatively; a numerical upper limit and its confidence level would improve clarity.

While the paper cites relevant phenomenology and Tcc+ theory broadly, explicit comparison with modern EFT-based treatments of near-threshold charm-meson molecules (e.g., XEFT-inspired) would sharpen the connection between extracted parameters and theoretical expectations.

A higher-level positioning relative to the broader exotic-hadrons literature (as summarized in 2207.14594) could be expanded, especially regarding how the scattering parameters compare across molecular candidates (e.g., X(3872)).

The MHD simulations are non-relativistic and omit explicit cosmic-ray transport, radiative losses, and anisotropic conduction; the reconnection-driven re-acceleration claim therefore rests on indirect evidence and numerical (implicit) resistivity.

The jet injection and magnetic-arch configuration are presented largely as a single fiducial setup; parameter-space exploration (e.g., dependence on magnetic field strength/geometry, jet power/velocity, viewing angle) is limited.

Polarization and Faraday rotation measurements, which could directly probe magnetic field ordering and strength along the cold front, are not presented; such data would be a powerful corroboration of the magnetic-layer hypothesis.

The spectral index analysis relies on broadband imaging, but systematics (absolute flux scale, beam mismatch, deconvolution biases, spectral curvature) and uncertainties are not quantified in detail; spectral aging or curvature modeling (JP/KP/tribble) is not attempted.

The X-ray evidence for a plasma depletion layer is suggestive but not quantified (e.g., significance of the deviation from the best-fit model, temperature structure across the discontinuity to confirm cold-front nature vs. shock).
A few inconsistencies/typos and unit ambiguities (e.g., ρ0 units listed as cm^-3 rather than g cm^-3; “Kelven-Helmholtz”), and inconsistent counts of sub-bands used for spectral mapping.
The physical plausibility of the adopted magnetic field amplitude (B1 ~ 60 μG) at the cold front could be motivated more clearly with observational constraints or scaling arguments.

While the paper cites foundational cold-front and WAT literature, a more explicit comparison to polarization/RM studies of cold fronts and jet bending in clusters would contextualize the magnetic-layer strengths and coherence scales assumed.
A quantitative contrast with the ram-pressure bending scenario (e.g., momentum flux vs. ram pressure estimates) would strengthen the case that magnetic tension is the dominant bending agent here.
Polarisation: only one epoch, single frequency, and EVPA not absolutely calibrated; no Faraday rotation analysis; limits physical interpretation of magnetic field geometry.
Kinematics: J2’s separation decreases from 2017 to 2018 despite an overall positive trend; this raises questions about component identification and (u,v) coverage effects.
The jet–ISM density estimate relies on several strong and uncertain assumptions (e.g., head area from a large half-opening angle, strong-shock βh ≈ β/4), with no stated uncertainties.

The revised black hole mass (down to 4.4 × 10^7 M☉) depends on beaming-corrected scaling relations that are debated for blazars (line selection, continuum contamination) and is a large shift from earlier estimates.
Absence of multi-frequency VLBI prevents spectral index mapping, core shift assessment, RM determination, and depolarisation analysis.
No phase-referenced astrometry; the core assumed stationary despite potential blending and opacity-related shifts, which could bias proper motion estimates.
Limited number of epochs post-2010 flare; the J1 “stationarity” is only marginally significant (μ = -0.006 ± 0.004 mas/yr).

Some equation numbering/notation inconsistencies and typographical issues (e.g., duplicated equation labels, ≥ rendering), and ambiguous statements (e.g., two different jet power values in the same paragraph).
The polarisation discussion occasionally implies magnetic field ordering without EVPA calibration or RM constraints; should be more tentative.
Limited comparison to polarisation properties at high rest frequencies in blazars and to young/GPS/CSS populations at similar redshifts.
Could better situate opening angle assumptions using recent MOJAVE distributions and discuss recollimation shocks as an internal alternative to ISM-triggered standing shocks.
Spatial correlation analyses with receptor maps do not appear to control for spatial autocorrelation (e.g., spin tests/BrainSMASH), risking inflated significance due to regional smoothness.

The insomnia classification dataset is modest in size (n≈101) and demographically different (older) than the discovery cohort, raising overfitting and cohort-shift concerns; hyperparameter tuning and nested CV details are limited.
Static RSFC only; no exploration of dynamic functional connectivity which may capture arousal/attentional fluctuations more sensitively.

Limited reporting on feature standardization and hyperparameter optimization within folds for SVR/SVM; risk of minor information leakage or optimistic estimates if preprocessing was not strictly nested.

The “significant edges” that form the biomarker are not fully specified in terms of selection/thresholding procedures (e.g., bootstrap ratios, multiple-comparison framework), hampering reproducibility and interpretability.
Potential clinical confounds (e.g., depression/anxiety, medications, sleep apnea) not clearly controlled in the insomnia dataset.
Minor terminology and typographical inconsistencies (e.g., Brainnetome/“Brainconnectome,” punctuation in atlas naming) and occasional grammatical slips that could be polished.
Effect sizes for prediction (r≈0.18) could be contextualized with additional performance metrics (MAE/RMSE) and calibration analyses for clearer practical interpretation.
Limited discussion of dynamic FC literature and its relevance to arousal/attention fluctuations in sleep health.
A more direct comparison with other sleep-disorder biomarkers (including EEG-based graph approaches) would help situate the gains and trade-offs across modalities and datasets.
Potential circularity: day/night periods are inferred from the same neural signal later used to quantify day–night differences, which may bias effect sizes and directionality.
Single narrowband sensing (±2 Hz around a clinician-chosen frequency) introduces selection bias and limits the ability to disentangle periodic peaks from aperiodic 1/f changes across subjects.
No explicit decomposition of periodic versus aperiodic components (e.g., FOOOF), which could confound conclusions about band-limited oscillations versus broadband arousal-related shifts.
Statistical analyses do not account for within-subject correlation between hemispheres; simple ANOVAs and non-parametric tests may overstate precision without mixed-effects modeling.

Absence of sleep staging or independent behavioral/physiological measures (actigraphy, polysomnography) for the full cohort limits the interpretability of “nighttime” effects and sleep-stage specificity.
STN subgroup is relatively small (n=30 hemispheres), reducing power to detect medication/stimulation interactions and limiting cross-target generalizability.

GLM covariates are limited; potential confounders (e.g., disease severity proxies beyond preop UPDRS, medication schedules/agonists, lead localization in motor territory, aperiodic slope) are not included.
The z-score normalization approach (±12 h window) may attenuate or distort circadian amplitudes; its impact on inferred differences is not quantified via sensitivity analyses.

Ambiguity in how z-scoring was computed (sliding vs global), how missing data and outliers were handled, and how significance for “no day–night difference” was determined given the day/night selection procedure.
Limited quantification of effect sizes (e.g., absolute/percent changes in power) and of within-subject reliability (day-to-day stability, cosine fits, or phase consistency).
The rationale for band definitions and grouping of variable center frequencies (especially near 13 Hz) could be better justified and sensitivity-tested.
While key PD sleep/DBS works are cited, there is little engagement with methods for circadian modeling from other domains (e.g., Bayesian circadian HMMs) that could improve state segmentation.
No discussion of separating oscillatory versus aperiodic LFP components despite relevance to arousal/sleep (common in EEG/iEEG literature).
Limited linkage to recent work on learning long-timescale neural dynamics that could inform adaptive control with time-of-day priors.

Rhythm isolation relies on band-pass filtering of band-power time series with limited methodological detail (filter type/order, phase handling, edge-treatment, handling of missing data), raising concerns about leakage and boundary effects, especially for long periods with short recordings.
The coarse binning of ultradian bands (e.g., 1–3 h, 3–6 h, etc.) may conflate episodic fluctuations with true rhythmicity and may not adapt to inter-individual variability in timescales.
Potential confounds include referencing scheme, contact type (depth vs subdural), SNR/impedance differences, distance to white matter, and spectral slope changes; these are only partially addressed.

Sleep/wake and sleep stage are not modeled, though they likely drive much of the circadian and ultradian band-power modulation; this raises interpretability concerns regarding whether diminished rhythms reflect altered local sleep physiology, a central point acknowledged but not probed with proxies.
Medication tapering, post-implant effects, hospital routines, and anesthesia can substantially modulate rhythms; there is no systematic control for these factors across days or subjects.

Heterogeneity in recording duration (2–21 days) impacts reliability of the longest periods; analyses do not clearly weight patients by number of observable cycles or assess per-subject confidence for each cycle band.

Independence of peri-ictal vs inter-ictal effects is assessed with rolling AUC and paired t-tests; given autocorrelation and unequal sample sizes, more robust nonparametric or mixed-effects approaches may be preferable.

Orientation of ROC/AUC labeling (what constitutes the positive class) is not completely transparent; stating explicitly why AUC>0.5 indicates diminished magnitude in pathological tissue would avoid confusion.
Details on artifact rejection, handling of dropouts, and whether seizures and high-IED-rate segments were excluded or modeled are sparse.
The mapping from contacts to ROIs and any within-ROI aggregation steps (median vs mean, weighting) need clearer exposition.

Limited methodological triangulation (e.g., cosinor, Lomb–Scargle periodograms for uneven sampling, wavelet/spectral peak analyses, or EMD/Hilbert-based approaches) to corroborate filter-based findings.

Broader positioning relative to literature on local sleep dynamics (local slow waves, regional sleep homeostasis) and network-level chronobiology in epilepsy could be better integrated to contextualize mechanisms.
Potential circularity/double-dipping in ROI selection: ROIs are derived from condition-sensitive EEG source contrasts then used to predict the same condition-specific phenomena.
The choice of HMM state number (K=4) is weakly justified; sensitivity to K and model selection criteria (e.g., free energy/BIC) are not reported.
Directionality (“PCU→V1 causal effect”) and phase coupling claims require stronger controls for volume conduction/leakage, common drivers (e.g., thalamus), and frequency specificity.
Lack of eye-tracking/OKN-based timing to disambiguate true perceptual transition times from report/motor latency; motor preparation confounds remain a concern for pre-report windows.
Potential contamination of pre-dominant windows by preceding perceptual states (acknowledged by authors) may differentially impact BR vs RPL interpretation.
Cross-validation details for classification based on state fractional occupancy (class balancing, leakage prevention, metrics) are not provided.
Insufficient detail on the spectral profiles of HMM states and the specific frequency bands implicated in PCU–V1 coupling; unclear whether results generalize across alpha/beta/gamma.
Ambiguity in terminology (e.g., “switching rate” vs “fractional occupancy”), and at times overreliance on AIC differences as significance evidence without effect sizes/confidence intervals.

Limited engagement with dynamical and thermodynamic frameworks of rivalry beyond mutual inhibition (e.g., landscape/flux perspectives), and with established model predictions about pre-switch trajectories.
No mention of OKN-based methods for precise, continuous percept estimation in rivalry, which could materially strengthen timing claims.

Reliance on 1D PIC may underrepresent key multidimensional kinetic effects (e.g., lower-hybrid drift, electron KH-like modes, tearing, turbulence) known to reshape current sheets and possibly alter orbit-class transitions.

The derivation of the short-time Vlasov response (Eq. 3–4) assumes a quasi-stationary background; a more careful delineation of its regime of validity and corrections as the profile evolves would strengthen the argument.

The assumption that early-time dynamics primarily produce NC → DW transitions while leaving M largely unaffected may not hold once fluctuations and profile curvature develop; a quantitative criterion for when M transitions remain subdominant is missing.

Missing simulation details (mass ratio, number of particles per cell, grid spacing, time step, boundary conditions, smoothing/filters, field solver, numerical heating checks) prevent assessment of numerical accuracy and reproducibility.
No parameter scan (e.g., different initial under-heating levels, λ/di, beta, guide/normal fields, mass ratio) is provided to test robustness and generality of the mechanism.

Lack of diagnostics that track orbit-class membership over time in the evolving fields; current identification is inferred from phase-space patterns rather than particle-tagging against evolving invariants.

Some notation and normalization choices (e.g., definition and interpretation of dimensionless parameters, consistency of tildes/bars across text and figures) could be made more explicit for reproducibility.
The Methods section appears truncated; orbit classification and PIC configuration need full detail.

Limited discussion of how multidimensional instabilities (electron-scale tearing vs shear/KH-like modes) interact with orbit-class transitions and bifurcation (see recent controlled PIC studies of thickness-dependent transitions at electron scales).
While the paper addresses several historical explanations, a more systematic juxtaposition with modern non-Maxwellian VDF impacts on kinetic processes would reinforce the “orbit-mixture” perspective.

Reliance on a 1D PIC setup precludes multidimensional effects (e.g., lower-hybrid drift, drift-kink, Kelvin–Helmholtz–type shear modes, LHDI) that often influence thin current-sheet relaxation paths and could modify or compete with the proposed orbit-class transition mechanism.

The study focuses on under-heated (ξ > 0) equilibrations; the converse case (over-heated sheets, ξ < 0) and the robustness of the mechanism across a parameter sweep (thickness, mass ratio, β, guide/normal fields) are not explored.
The degree to which self-consistent electric fields and deviations from φ = 0 during relaxation affect the transition pathways is not fully quantified.

Simulation details (domain size, boundary conditions, particles per cell, mass ratio, c/ωpe, smoothing/filters) and numerical convergence tests are not fully documented, limiting reproducibility and quantitative assessment.
No direct, quantitative accounting of class population transfer fractions versus time; the evidence is compelling visually but would benefit from explicit tracking metrics.

The derivation and applicability limits of the short-time response (Eq. 3–4) could be more thoroughly contextualized, especially around when nonlinear self-consistency invalidates the linearized picture and how this impacts predicted transition rates.
The criteria for orbit classification in terms of invariants could be summarized compactly (e.g., a pz–v⊥ decision diagram) to aid readers applying the method elsewhere.

The paper would benefit from a more explicit quantitative connection to curvature-scattering frameworks and κ-parameter diagnostics widely used in magnetotail studies, and from discussing heavy-ion (e.g., O+) contributions known to produce bifurcation via different mechanisms.
A broader observational context beyond a single MMS event (e.g., statistics or multiple events with/without reconnection) would strengthen claims of generality.

The geometric forward model represents kink boundary motion via modulation of the minor radius in a torus parameterisation rather than explicit rigid displacement of the loop cross-section; the physical fidelity of this approximation is not fully justified.
Intensity formation and line-of-sight integration effects (column depth changes) are neglected, though these can subtly affect apparent displacements and phase.

The conclusion that random footpoint driving necessarily implies random polarisation is asserted but not quantitatively demonstrated; boundary and structural anisotropies could bias the polarisation in practice.
Potential artifacts or biases from motion magnification are not systematically quantified (e.g., amplitude linearity, phase integrity across magnification factors 5–10).
The analysis focuses on apex-near slits averaged over narrow spatial bands; a systematic survey of phase consistency along the loop and across time windows with uncertainty propagation is limited.
No spectroscopic constraints (e.g., Doppler phase or line-width diagnostics) are used to corroborate the POS-based polarisation inference and rule out multi-thread or LOS superposition effects.
Uncertainty estimates for key derived quantities (phase lag, hodogram axis ratios, Gaussian σ of minor axes) are not consistently reported with confidence intervals or error propagation.
Some terminology (e.g., “horizontal” vs “oblique” relative to the loop plane and the two instrument PoS) could benefit from a single schematic defining all angles and planes in one place.
Recent single-instrument hodogram approaches combining POS and Doppler velocities to infer polarisation (e.g., CoMP-based methods) could be discussed as complementary and cross-validating techniques.
State-of-the-art 3D MHD simulations showing sustained decayless oscillations under red-noise footpoint driving could nuance the interpretation that random driving predicts random polarisation.

Redshifts and masses rely solely on photometry to 4.4 μm; without spectroscopic confirmation or longer‑wavelength constraints (e.g., MIRI, ALMA), residual degeneracies with dusty/line‑dominated SEDs and AGN components remain.

The paper removes very dusty templates (AV ~ 3) from EAZY to avoid unconstrained M/L inflation at rest λ < 0.5 μm, but this also reduces the template flexibility and may bias mass inferences if dustier solutions are physically present.
Structural size claims (re ≤ 0.5 kpc) are at or below the F444W PSF scale at z ~ 8–10; sizes are likely unresolved or strongly PSF‑dominated.

Cosmic variance and completeness are not quantified; number/mass densities are presented as sums over the surveyed comoving volume, but selection functions, Vmax, and Eddington bias corrections are not rigorously modeled.

Lensing analysis is cursory (nearest‑neighbor Einstein‑radius check). Weak magnification from line‑of‑sight structure could systematically boost fluxes by ~10–30% and is not incorporated into the uncertainty budget.
The mass‑uncertainty propagation to mass density uses a simple factor‑of‑3 Monte Carlo; a full forward model coupling photometric errors, SED systematics, and selection incompleteness is missing.

The comparison to prior mass densities occasionally reads as categorical; several claims would benefit from explicit error bars that include cosmic variance, completeness, lensing, and SPS systematics.
The statement that re ≤ 0.5 kpc galaxies are “extremely compact” should acknowledge PSF limitations and present PSF‑corrected upper limits rather than nominal sizes.

The discussion could better contextualize tensions with empirical/theoretical models that reproduce high‑z UV LFs within ΛCDM but predict more modest stellar mass densities; for example, recent UniverseMachine‑based work argues that some extreme masses may arise from SED systematics (dust, AGN, SPS/IMF assumptions).

Potential biases when using NIRCam‑only SEDs in dusty systems (e.g., dust‑obscuration bias) and the role of IMF systematics (e.g., bottom‑heavy IMFs implied in older quiescents) merit brief discussion of how they could alter inferred masses.

Neutral gas constraints rely on the optically thin approximation and a fixed Na I neutral fraction (1 − y = 0.1), with the Na I D doublet unresolved at R ~ 1000; the absence of a partial covering doublet model (τ–Cf degeneracy) likely underestimates systematic uncertainties on N(Na I) and hence Ṁ_out.
The neutral outflow radius is assumed equal to the ionized outflow radius (3 kpc); absorption cannot directly constrain R_out and Ṁ scales linearly with it.
Electron density n_e is assumed (500 cm−3) for ionized mass estimates with ±0.7 dex systematics; [S II]/[O II] diagnostics are too uncertain to constrain n_e directly.
BPT classification is complicated because some lines (e.g., [O III], Hβ) are dominated by outflowing gas rather than the NLR/ISM; this may bias AGN diagnostics and bolometric inferences.
Energetics and momentum budget are not quantitatively compared to the putative AGN luminosity and to SNe-driven expectations; such a comparison would strongly buttress the AGN-driven conclusion.
Coverage fraction (Cf) of absorbing gas is inferred qualitatively (>50%) but is not fit explicitly; assuming Cf = 1 simplifies but can bias N(H I) estimates.
The reliance on polynomial spectral distortion and a global slit-loss correction (~2×) is sensible but could more clearly quantify how this impacts absolute line luminosities and derived masses.
The large uncertainty on [N II] flux and fixed Hα kinematics may bias BPT placement; an explicit sensitivity analysis on the BPT coordinates would help.

Recent JWST-based Na D neutral-outflow studies at z ~ 1–3 (e.g., population-level Blue Jay Na D incidence and mass-loading; post-starburst/quiescent fossil-outflow cases) could be discussed more thoroughly to position this object within emerging trends.
A brief comparison to IFU-based high-z ionized-outflow studies without AGN (e.g., GA-NIFS) would further emphasize why the ionized phase alone often appears inefficient.
Mapping from drug dose/receptor occupancy to model parameters (e.g., Δτi, Δτe, be changes) is qualitative rather than quantitatively calibrated to pharmacodynamics/pharmacokinetics.

NMDA antagonism is modeled solely as a decreased excitatory decay time τe; ketamine’s network effects (e.g., gamma increases, layer-specific actions, disinhibition) can be more complex and circuit-dependent.
The thalamus and thalamocortical loops are not explicitly modeled, despite their known roles in anesthesia- and sleep-related slow oscillations.
Whole-brain analyses use a single (group-average) connectome and one parcellation; robustness across connectomes, atlases, and conduction velocity/delay choices is not assessed.
The SC–FC analysis lacks controls for potential confounds (e.g., motion, arousal fluctuations, global signal regression choices), and the sample size is inconsistently reported (39 vs 26 subjects).
PCI is computed from firing rates rather than forward-modeled EEG/MEG signals; the thresholding and source-entropy normalization are adapted but not validated against sensor-level PCI.
Minor inconsistencies and typos hinder precision (e.g., “N = 104” likely means 10^4 neurons; 39 vs 26 subjects; occasional switch between Te and τe).
Parameter settings that differ across conditions (e.g., vdrive, global coupling) are not always fully justified, making it hard to disentangle mechanism- vs regime-dependent effects.
Limited quantitative comparison to alternative node models and formulations (e.g., Wilson–Cowan, Hopf, adaptive linear–nonlinear mean-field) regarding robustness of the inferred mechanisms.

Empirical literature indicating potentially distinct PCI effects among anesthetics (e.g., dissociative ketamine vs GABAergic agents) is not fully reconciled with the model’s finding of no significant differences between anesthetic mechanisms.

PAC estimation can be confounded by non-sinusoidal waveforms and transient events (e.g., spikes), and MI significance thresholds or surrogate/analytic nulls are not systematically applied per contact; this limits interpretability of MI magnitude differences relative to potential spurious PAC.
Referencing scheme (e.g., common average, bipolar) and filtering details are not fully specified; both materially affect HFO and MI estimates and may vary across centers or ages.

The tractography analysis is descriptive and uses population-averaged DWI templates; no statistical test links MI co-growth strength to tract density beyond visualization, thus causal inferences about structure–function coupling remain tentative.

The cohort comprises only epilepsy patients with ILAE 1 outcomes; even with “nonepileptic” site selection, generalizability to healthy development is uncertain, and residual pathology or network-level effects may persist.

Sleep staging is identified via visual selection of slow-wave epochs rather than standardized polysomnographic scoring (N2 vs N3); state heterogeneity (and night-to-night variability) is not quantified.

Sensitivity analyses for detector parameter choices, referencing, artifact rejection, and epoch length are limited; findings (e.g., occipital elevation) show detector dependence in the youngest group.

Sampling bias due to clinically driven electrode coverage is unavoidable; the atlas interpolates within 10 mm, but nonuniform coverage could bias regional developmental slopes without explicit coverage-weighting or sampling maps in the main text.
Inconsistencies between uncorrected and FDR-corrected p-values across sections can confuse interpretation; clearer, uniform reporting of corrected significance would help.
The rationale for prioritizing HIL-based HFO rates (beyond alignment with MI computation) could be more explicitly justified given detector discrepancies.

PAC pitfalls and bispectral alternatives are not directly addressed; leveraging analytic null distributions for MI or comparisons to bispectral estimators would strengthen claims (e.g., Aru et al., 2015; Lozano‑Soldevilla et al., 2017).
External validation against larger multi-center resources (e.g., Omni-iEEG) or independent cohorts is not attempted; even partial validation would support generalizability.
Limited theoretical analysis: lacks a stability/wave-number selection theory linking delays, synaptic time constants, and connectivity to predicted wavelengths and speeds.
LFP modeling is simplified (summed synaptic currents plus post-hoc smoothing), omitting volume conduction, laminar mixing, and biophysics that could influence wave detection/metrics.

Inhibitory/excitatory pathway asymmetries (e.g., different spatial extents, synaptic kinetics, and conduction speeds) are not systematically explored, though these are known to shape cortical dynamics.
Sparse participation is central, yet a quantitative “participation index” (fraction of neurons engaged per wave, distribution over space/time) is not explicitly defined or compared to data.

Correlation analyses rely primarily on spike-spike coherence and a global pairwise metric; distance-dependent noise correlations and count correlations across time windows would strengthen the AI claim under waves.
Model–data comparison for wavelength and speed is described as close, but quantitative goodness-of-fit metrics (e.g., KS distances, likelihood-based fits) are not reported.

Some parameters critically shaping dynamics (synaptic time constants, inhibitory delays vs excitatory, refractory periods) are not front-and-center; clearer parameter tables and sensitivity analyses would help reproducibility.
Boundary conditions and edge-handling are briefly mentioned (outer mm discarded) but their effects on wave statistics are not characterized.

Prior theoretical/simulation literature on traveling waves in spatially extended E/I networks with delays (e.g., Roxin–Brunel–Hansel, Ermentrout/Pinto line, rate/phase-reduced analyses) could be engaged more deeply to situate the contribution.

Recent computational platforms enabling large-scale spiking simulations (e.g., NEST GPU onboard instantiation; differentiable simulators like BrainPy) and spiking ML literature on learnable delays and topography provide relevant context for scalability and broader implications.

Field modeling for stimulation appears simplified: SEEG stimulation is mapped via sensor-to-source proximity/decay rather than full patient-specific FEM/EIT solutions with anisotropic conductivities; TI field computation details are insufficient to assess physical fidelity (e.g., tissue conductivities, boundary conditions, anisotropy, and envelope derivation).

The Epileptor-Stimulation coupling (how E-field modulates “m,” thresholds, and parameter scaling) lacks explicit equations and biophysical justification/calibration against empirical stimulation thresholds or afterdischarge phenomena.
Identifiability of parameters and sensitivity to modeling choices (priors, coupling gains, connectivity uncertainties) are not analyzed.

Validation is largely circular: synthetic ictal data are generated from the same model instantiated with the assumed EZ, and the inversion recovers that EZ. This demonstrates internal consistency but not external validity on real stimulation-induced seizures.

No quantitative comparison to alternative EZ mapping approaches (spectral biomarkers, data-driven inference, or other model-based methods), nor ablations isolating benefits of high-resolution modeling or multimodal inversion.
Robustness analyses (noise, electrode localization errors, montage variation, tractography variability, prior mis-specification) are missing.
No computational performance profile (HMC settings, convergence diagnostics, runtime, scalability) is provided.
Critical mathematical details (Epileptor-Stimulation equation(s), likelihood/data-feature definition, multimodal likelihood fusion) are deferred or absent, making replication difficult.
Minor typographical inconsistencies (e.g., “measial,” “Fl,” “forth”) and figure OCR artifacts impede precision in some places.
Limited engagement with recent advances in TI field modeling and optimization (e.g., FEM-based montage design, safety/SAR constraints) and broader perturbational modeling literature.
No discussion of safety/feasibility bounds (current intensities, envelope thresholds, charge density at SEEG contacts, TI heating/SAR), which are essential for clinical translation.
Causality remains unproven: analyses are largely correlational; the negative feedback of LoWS on IED-related HG is inferred, not perturbed.
LoWS detection relies on band-limited filtering and amplitude/duration thresholds (90th percentile); sensitivity analyses to these choices are limited.
Wakefulness/drowsiness is not physiologically tracked (e.g., EOG, EMG, pupillometry), raising the possibility of micro-sleep confounds.
IED detection involves semi-automated plus manual curation; subjectivity and inter-rater reliability are not quantified.
Comparisons with Parkinson’s disease recordings use different brain regions and modalities (neocortical ECoG vs mesial temporal depth), complicating interpretation of differences.
The linear mixed model using “time-to-next-IED” as a dependent variable may not optimally capture event hazard; survival/point-process models could be more appropriate.
Limited assessment of covariates (medication state, time-of-day, prior sleep, arousal) that could influence LoWS/IED dynamics.
Trial-level behavioral analyses could be strengthened with tighter temporal alignment between LoWS occurrence and response times.
The “corrected rate” of LoWS defined by multiplying by IED rate is unconventional; a regression-based adjustment may be more interpretable.
Some model specifications (random effects structure, handling of within-electrode dependence, multicollinearity checks) are not fully detailed.
Definitions of slope and amplitude, while present, could benefit from a compact schematic and justification relative to sleep SW metrics.
Limited engagement with formal hazard modeling of epileptiform events and point-process approaches common in computational neuroscience.

Could further connect to prior intracranial literature on “local sleep” in humans and the low-theta/delta distinction, and to higher-order interaction metrics (e.g., interaction information) that have mapped epileptogenic networks.

Interaction strength is manipulated indirectly (nutrient additions presumed to amplify competitive modification of media); direct quantification of interaction coefficients or environmental mediation (e.g., pH profiles) in the present study is limited.

The gLV model with random interactions and constant immigration captures emergent regimes but abstracts away resource mediation and facilitation; generality beyond competition-dominated settings is not fully demonstrated.

The primary resident-community panel (17 communities) yields a relatively small number of successful invasions (9 total), making some correlations fragile; multiple testing corrections and mixed-effects modeling are not reported.

Invaders are re-introduced daily post-day 6 (propagule pressure) but its potential interaction with stability/dynamics is not systematically varied; this could bias invasion probabilities upward and complicate mapping to theory with a single immigration parameter.
Use of 16S relative abundances to define invasion success (threshold 8×10^-4) can be sensitive to compositional effects; absolute abundance controls or spike-ins are not reported.

The precise criteria and diagnostics used to classify “stable” vs. “fluctuating” states are deferred to the supplement; main-text clarity would benefit from a succinct summary of the classifier and timescale considerations.

The term “universal” for the survival-fraction relationship is strong given deviations under strong interactions and the modest number of experimental conditions; tempering or providing uncertainty bands would aid interpretation.
Limited discussion of resource-explicit alternatives (consumer–resource models) and how they might alter the phase structure and priority effects.

Connections to post-antibiotic alternative stable states and long-lived perturbations documented in human gut datasets could be expanded, as these observations resonate with the priority-effect findings.
The analysis relies on relative-abundance inputs; compositional constraints can induce spurious correlations and bias feature importance unless properly transformed or controlled.
The approach assumes identically distributed assembly rules and stationarity across local communities; out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., new geographies, diets, lab conditions) is not tested.
No explicit treatment of multistability or inoculum-size thresholds, despite their relevance to invasion ecology and clinical engraftment.
Neural ODE components add limited practical gain over simpler models here; the claimed benefit of NODEs is not systematically established.
Absolute biomass and environmental covariates (e.g., antibiotic identity, medium composition) are not explicitly modeled in predictors; antibiotic pretreatment could confound model attributions.
Colonization-impact inference perturbs inputs but may push outside the empirical manifold; no sensitivity analysis or regularization to remain within plausible ecological states.
The high invader dose (5%) may not reflect clinically relevant inocula and could mask threshold effects or early stochastic establishment dynamics.
Generalization to in vivo settings (host immunity, mucosal niches) is untested; conclusions are limited to in vitro ecosystems.
Details of COP-NODE architectures, hyperparameters, and training protocols are not fully specified; it is hard to reproduce or assess why Random Forests consistently outperform NODEs.
The precise computation of colonization impact (perturbation magnitude, normalization, evaluation protocol) should be specified more rigorously.
Comparisons to strong nonparametric baselines (e.g., gradient-boosted trees, kernel methods, EDM) and to mechanistic prediction using inferred GLV/MiCRM parameters are absent.

The work could be better contextualized relative to recent mechanistic invasion theories that yield closed-form post-invasion states and feedback-corrected fitness (e.g., dressed invasion fitness frameworks), clarifying complementarity and trade-offs.
The definition of “QS receptors” is too broad: counting generic two-component systems (TCS) as QS receptors risks substantial over-calling, since many TCSs sense environmental cues unrelated to QS.
Classifier features are limited to 20 amino-acid composition frequencies, which are unlikely to capture QS-specific signatures and are prone to learning taxonomic biases rather than function.
The term “ensemble classifiers” is used, but the work appears to train four separate models without a principled ensemble/consensus scheme or calibration.
Performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) are referenced but not reported numerically; confusion matrices, ROC/PR curves, or calibration plots are missing.

Potential homology/annotation leakage: positives and negatives come from overlapping proteomes, and candidates are pre-filtered via BLASTP with a moderate E-value; a genus/species-held-out evaluation is not provided.
No benchmarking against strong domain-baseline methods (e.g., Pfam/InterPro HMMs for LuxI/LuxR, RpfF, PqsABCD/MvfR, LuxS/LsrB, AgrCA/peptides, ComDE/ComC).
Ambiguity in thresholds (e.g., “E value 105” likely means 1e−5), and “ensemble classifiers” terminology is confusing.
The mapping from predicted proteins to specific QS languages is insufficiently specified, particularly when labeling receptors to languages beyond canonical systems.
Limited discussion of domain/HMM-based QS detection and gene-cluster-level criteria that are commonly used for QS system identification.
No quantitative comparison against simple BLAST/HMM pipelines to isolate the incremental value of the ML classifiers.

The automated kcat “up-shifting” to the class maximum until growth matches an experimental target risks unrealistic kinetics and overfitting to growth rate, potentially biasing downstream predictions.

Exclusive reliance on Homo sapiens entries for ecHuman1 kcat assignment may be insufficient to populate tens of thousands of reactions; the feasibility and coverage of this choice need clearer justification and quantitative evidence.
The definition and handling of enzyme “saturation” metrics, particularly under constraint loosening or exclusion of incompatible proteomics entries, may confound interpretation of enzyme usage.

Limited benchmarking beyond growth-rate and gas-exchange metrics; little use of 13C fluxomics or independent enzyme activity/protein allocation datasets to validate internal predictions and claimed isoenzyme diversification effects.
The E. coli comparison uses a single ME-model and an SSE measure without detailed error normalization; broader baselines (e.g., MOMENT, RBA variants) and richer metrics would strengthen claims.
Lack of runtime and scalability characterization for the new FVA module and proteomics-integration workflow on the largest models (e.g., Human1).

Critical algorithmic details (phylogenetic distance measure, thresholds, unit conversion from specific activity to kcat, exact rules for loosening proteomics constraints) are deferred to supplementary materials and could be summarized more explicitly in the main text for reproducibility.
Calibration steps in the CI pipeline (e.g., how growth targets are applied, how re-calibration is handled upon upstream GEM changes) are not described with sufficient procedural detail.
While ME and RBA are discussed, there is limited quantitative comparison against other enzyme-capacity FBA variants (e.g., MOMENT, CAFBA, recent ecFBA pipelines).

The relationship to dynamic resource-allocation frameworks (e.g., dynamic eukaryotic RBA/dRBA) is not explored; the differences in data requirements, scope (steady-state vs dynamic), and trade-offs could be articulated to contextualize GECKO 2.0’s niche.

The dataset is very small (28 entries) relative to the chemical-design space, raising overfitting risk and limiting generalizability; 10-fold CV on n≈29 (including baseline) yields folds of size ~3 with potentially high variance.

The current feature representation treats a binary additive as a concentration-normalized sum of atomic descriptors, which may miss crucial higher-order interactions between functional groups and does not explicitly capture cross-additive synergies.

The decision to fix candidate dual-additive compositions to 1 wt% each during screening leaves composition optimization on the table; optimal loading and ratio are likely important and may be non-monotonic.
The reported MAEs for ASI and ΔASI (≈20 and ≈15 Ω·cm² on test folds) are large compared with the baseline and improvement margins, potentially blurring rank-ordering confidence.
Replicate counts, variability, and statistical significance of improvements are not reported; given known EIS and cycling variability, this is critical to support the claimed gains.
Grouped cross-validation (e.g., leave-one-additive-out or leave-one-scaffold-out) is not performed; sample-wise CV may leak additive identity across train/test and inflate apparent performance.
The final metrics (e.g., cycle number for “final” ASI, ΔASI, Q; formation and cycling protocols; temperature; EIS fitting procedure) are not fully specified in the main text.

Selection of the six validation candidates relies primarily on ΔASI and Q due to perceived model reliability, but a principled multi-objective/uncertainty-aware selection (e.g., Pareto fronts with expected hypervolume improvement) would better reflect trade-offs.
Table 1 contains clear errors: duplicated entry number “32” with radically different metrics; numbering inconsistencies (e.g., two “32” rows) undermine trust in reporting.

The “MS” acronym and structures appear inconsistent across text and Figure 2 (e.g., the figure transcription shows a LiFSI-like anion labeled “MS,” while the text describes “malonato tetrafluorophosphates”); this needs immediate clarification.
The Spearman correlation discussion sometimes reads inconsistently with the sign/direction in the plotted lists; clearer reconciliations and cautions about small-sample correlations are needed.

A statement that “SEM confirms the presence of TM aggregates in cells with additives, thereby reducing their detrimental effects” is confusing—why would aggregates reduce harm? This needs mechanistic clarification or rewording.

The paper cites relevant ML-for-electrolyte works but does not position its approach against recent closed-loop/robotic optimization and multi-objective discovery frameworks (e.g., Clio, ALBATROSS, Bayesian optimization in Otto/Dragonfly) in terms of methodology and throughput.
No benchmarking against alternative models (RF, SVR, XGBoost, multi-task GPs) or feature ablations is shown to justify GPR + the chosen descriptors as the best low-data choice.

Electrochemical window (ECW) estimation from gas-phase HOMO/LUMO levels is known to be unreliable and systematically overestimates oxidative stability; no solvation/condensed-phase corrections or explicit referencing to Li|Li+ are used.
Classification metrics are reported as “R²” for categorical tasks; appropriate metrics (accuracy, ROC-AUC, F1, precision/recall) and calibrated probabilities are missing.

Details of data curation and leakage control are insufficient: it is unclear whether IL-wise splits prevent the same IL (or same cation/anion family) from appearing in both train and test, which can inflate performance under sparse labels.
Inconsistencies and ambiguities in sample counts (e.g., 1240 vs 1084 liquids) raise questions about the exact training/labeling protocol and the temperature normalization for σ at RT.

tLi+ via Bruce–Vincent can be error-prone in concentrated IL/polymer systems; independent validation (e.g., eNMR, concentration-cell, or modern polarization-with-correction methods) would strengthen transport claims.

No quantification of Li content or ionic composition in the membranes (e.g., ICP-OES, elemental analysis, NMR), despite one IL failing to exchange Li; mechanistic claims about PBDT–ion interactions lack direct evidence.

Limited interphase diagnostics (e.g., XPS/TOF-SIMS of SEI/CEI, impedance evolution) to link stability to specific chemistries; mechanical properties (modulus, toughness, creep) of the membranes are not reported.

Hydrophilicity/processability constraints (aqueous casting) were applied post hoc during IL selection; these constraints are not part of the ML screen and thus reduce the end-to-end optimality of the pipeline.
Misrendered symbols (σ as “o”) and notational inconsistencies complicate interpretation; several equations lack unit/reference details.
GCN architecture and representation of cation–anion pairs (single combined graph? dual-graph fusion?) are not sufficiently specified to ensure reproducibility.
The rationale for the 5 mS cm⁻¹ threshold and its sensitivity analysis are not provided; ECW cutoff selection (3.5 V) is not justified against application-specific requirements.

No comparison against transfer-learning approaches that leverage COSMO-RS or MD pretraining to combat data sparsity (e.g., Sethi et al., 2509.10273), or recent multi-objective generative pipelines for electrolytes (e.g., conditional diffusion models).
Lack of ablations disentangling the value of Psi4 features versus purely topological/descriptor baselines, or of GCNs versus XGBoost under leakage-free splits.
No uncertainty quantification to guide experimental selection, despite the sparse/noisy label regime typical for ILs.

The LCE is trained on a relatively small set of 32 unique NEB hops; extrapolation across all local compositions may under-represent rare but rate-limiting local motifs or long-range electrostatics not captured in a local model.
Barriers are computed at 0 K on static lattices; vibrational free energy contributions, phonon-assisted effects, and temperature-dependent saddle-point softening are not explicitly included.
The framework focuses on bulk transport; grain-boundary, porosity, space-charge, and pellet/electrode contact effects that strongly affect EIS-derived conductivities are not modeled.
The assumption of random Si/P distributions based on high-T MC may not capture possible short-range ordering or synthesis-dependent polyanion clustering that can impact percolation.

Details on impedance analysis (bulk versus grain-boundary separation, electrode blocking behavior, fitting model and confidence intervals) are not fully elaborated; without this, quantitative comparison to bulk kMC predictions may be confounded by microstructural contributions.

The extent of experimental validation is limited to a subset of compositions; independent confirmation of predicted Haven ratios or tracer diffusivities via NMR/QENS would strengthen claims about correlated motion.

The kMC rate construction with KRA requires knowledge of endpoint energy differences to reconstruct directional barriers; it is unclear how site (Na(1)/Na(2)) energies were parameterized and whether a separate energetic CE was used.

Uncertainty quantification is limited: variance across polyanion configurations is partly shown (confidence band), but systematic error bars combining DFT barrier uncertainty, LCE fit errors, and kMC sampling noise are not fully propagated to σ and D.

The manuscript could better relate to contemporary strategies for barrier prediction and path enumeration (e.g., high-throughput NEB and ML-assisted NEB) and to multiscale treatments of grain-boundary effects in solid electrolytes, to position the present bulk-focused approach in the broader landscape.

A clearer discussion contrasting center-of-mass diffusivity–based conductivities with tracer-based measures and how these map to different experimental probes (EIS vs NMR/QENS) would help interpret Haven ratios and comparisons.

The “variational EM” formulation is not fully specified: the probabilistic model, latent variables, variational family, and the ELBO or monotonicity guarantees are not clearly defined; the procedure risks being perceived as heuristic alternating training rather than bona fide EM.
It remains unclear how uncertainty is handled or propagated across scales, especially important when one scale (e.g., structure) is predicted (AlphaFold) and potentially noisy.

Key details about datasets, negative sampling, leakage controls, and data preprocessing (e.g., use of predicted vs. experimental structures, homolog filtering, cross-protein family splits) are missing or under-specified.

Comparisons omit several strong modern baselines (e.g., models using protein language model embeddings, large-scale heterogeneous graph link predictors, gradient-balanced multi-task training methods like GradNorm/PCGrad/MGDA).
Robustness analyses are limited: performance under missing/inaccurate structures, cold-start entities (new proteins or drugs), or domain shift is not reported.
Loss functions, optimization schedule, and the specific mapping of E- and M-steps to modules and parameters are insufficiently detailed to reproduce results or scrutinize the EM claim.
Architectural details of the structural encoder and network-level predictor, hyperparameters, and convergence diagnostics are not presented in the provided text.

The manuscript could better contextualize against co-training/co-EM literature, multi-task optimization balancing methods, and recent multi-scale protein modeling approaches (e.g., integrating protein language models with structure and network information).
Discussion of biases and known pitfalls in DDI/PPI datasets (e.g., hub bias, redundancy, dataset construction artifacts) and how the method mitigates them is brief or absent.

Use of features within one year of diagnosis (e.g., NSAID prescriptions) likely captures prodromal symptom management rather than antecedent risk, inflating apparent predictiveness for early diagnosis rather than incident risk.
Median imputation without missingness indicators may bias associations; correlated-feature SHAP attributions can be unstable and misinterpreted without complementary checks.
Model type is binary classification over a fixed horizon; survival analysis or landmarking might better leverage censoring and temporal dynamics.

Calibration metrics (e.g., calibration plots, Brier score), decision-curve analysis, and comparison to strong, simple baselines (e.g., logistic regression with age+sex+BMI) are not reported, limiting assessment of clinical utility.
External validation is temporal but not external in population or health system; generalizability to non-UK settings and non-European ancestries is unclear.
Cluster stability (e.g., bootstrap stability, ARI/NMI across resamples) and rule robustness are not quantified; overlap/coverage–specificity tradeoffs of rules need fuller reporting.
Limited discussion of how class balancing (1:1 matched cases/controls) affects PPV/NPV under real-world prevalence; translational implications of thresholds and recalibration are underexplored.
Omics subset selection and potential sampling bias (age/sex/healthier volunteer bias) are acknowledged but not rigorously characterized.
Survival-model baselines (e.g., RSF or Cox) and explainable survival-to-classification mappings, as explored in recent EHR studies, are not compared.
PRS interpretability/uncertainty and cross-ancestry transportability advances are not engaged; methods such as BRIGHT or uncertainty-aware PRS could contextualize the limited WGPRS value observed.

Multi-label generation is implemented via an arbitrary within-visit ordering (priority order), which can introduce inductive bias and dependence on documentation practices; set-prediction or orderless decoding alternatives are not explored.

Decoding details are under-specified (e.g., teacher forcing vs. free-running during pretraining, end-of-visit termination token, handling the variable number of codes), and potential exposure-bias mitigation is not discussed.
Interpretability is lightly treated; reliance on attention weights as “top indicators” is known to be unstable and insufficient for clinical explanation without additional analyses.

The self-harm cohort description is confusing: the text lists 1,342 cases and 281 controls but also states a 1.9% prevalence among 70,967 PTSD patients; it is unclear which sample is used for model training/evaluation and what the actual class balance is.

Statistical testing uses a one-sided t-test across random seeds; this treats runs as independent samples of the data-generating process and may not accurately capture uncertainty. Better approaches include paired bootstrap or DeLong tests (for AUROC) and bootstrap for AUPRC with per-patient resampling.
Calibration (e.g., reliability curves, Brier score) and decision-analytic metrics (e.g., net benefit/decision curves) are not reported, which are essential for clinical deployment.
External validation is limited (ICU-only MIMIC-IV ICD-10 subset with modest gains); no zero-shot transfer is shown and broader multi-institutional generalization remains unproven.
Important implementation specifics (vocabulary size, ICD code granularity, hierarchy handling, label smoothing, loss formulation for multi-label generation) are missing, limiting reproducibility.
The term “Enformer” is already widely associated with a genomics foundation model; name reuse risks confusion in the literature and searchability.

The paper positions the approach as the first encoder–decoder generative framework for EHR next-visit multi-label prediction; however, subsequent/contemporaneous work (e.g., RAVEN and other next-visit generative EHR foundation models) has closely related objectives and should be discussed and, where possible, compared.

Strong structured baselines beyond LR/LSTM (e.g., LightGBM/TabPFN on ontology-rolled, time-binned counts) often remain competitive on EHR tasks; including such baselines would strengthen empirical claims.
Safety alignment measures are relatively narrow (e.g., blocking package installation) and do not yet constitute a comprehensive, formally verified safety architecture for AFM operation.
The planner–tool interface appears permissive; there is limited evidence of robust precondition checks, formal state machines, or typed parameter contracts to prevent unsafe motion or mode switches.
The optimization objective for PID tuning (SSIM of trace/retrace) may bias toward over-smoothing; no comparative analysis with alternative image-quality or stability metrics is provided.
Only two closed-source LLMs (GPT-4o and GPT-3.5-turbo-0125) are evaluated; there is no comparison to strong open-source models, non-LLM baselines (e.g., rule-based controllers), or human experts.

Statistical reporting is limited: averages are given without confidence intervals, dispersion, or formal significance tests; tool categories with few tasks (e.g., only four for Image Optimizer) are underpowered.
The “multi-agent coordination” degradation indicated in the abstract is not quantified with per-category success rates, ablations, or protocol-level analysis.
Efficiency times appear to emphasize agent/tool reasoning latency rather than end-to-end experimental duration that includes hardware overhead, limiting practical interpretability.
Some claims in the abstract seem stronger than supported by the results (e.g., “struggle even with basic documentation retrieval” versus reported 92%/72% success).
Terminology around “total errors” vs “error rate” and counts per category could be clarified; the donut labels and text occasionally give mixed signals without denominators.
“Mechanical property measurement” is claimed, but demonstrations mainly show roughness and friction in volts; there is no evidence of calibrated modulus or lateral force in SI units.
Limited discussion of recent autonomous SPM frameworks that use deep learning for defect detection, tip repair, and drift compensation at atomic resolution (Related Work: 2404.11162).
