Electrical characterization uses a two-electrode method over a fixed gap; contact resistance and geometry effects could confound true conductivity trends.

The grading-based SVM reports high overall accuracy, but class imbalance and per-class metrics (e.g., precision/recall, F1 for A vs. B/C) are not reported; calibration (e.g., Platt scaling) of SVM probabilities is not discussed despite use of probability thresholds.
Mechanical testing details (strain rate, sample geometry, anisotropy from freeze-drying) and long-term cycling/fatigue tests are not reported despite the wearable application.

Microstructural quantification (porosity/density by gravimetry, tomography; network morphology by SEM) is not systematically linked to mechanical/electrical outcomes, limiting mechanistic interpretability.
The use of mean relative error for log(R0) is unconventional and may obscure error magnitudes; additional metrics (R2, RMSE, calibration curves) would help.
Domain of applicability and extrapolation behavior of the ANN are not quantified; this is central for safe inverse design recommendations.
There is limited benchmarking against alternative small-data regressors with calibrated uncertainty (e.g., Gaussian Processes, ensembles) or Bayesian optimization for multi-objective inverse design.

Comparison to recent self-driving/agentic AI platforms and inverse-design techniques for porous media (e.g., property-conditional VAE, agentic toolchains) is not fully elaborated, and electromechanical stability comparisons to strain-invariant conductive aerogels (e.g., PEDOT:PSS frameworks with nanoscale encapsulation) are absent.

Potential confounding from climate and environmental gradients: key climate variables were removed when collinear with yield/suitability, risking attribution of climate-driven biodiversity patterns to yield.

Space-for-time substitution and reliance on observational associations limit causal interpretation; intensification is proxied by yield, which itself reflects multiple, heterogeneous management pathways.
Potential spatial autocorrelation in residuals is not explicitly modeled (e.g., spatial random effects or autocovariates), which can bias standard errors and effect sizes.
Stepwise model selection via likelihood-ratio tests can inflate Type I error and yields unstable model structures relative to information-criterion or regularization-based approaches.
No explicit out-of-sample validation or predictive performance metrics to assess generalizability.

The expansion scenario assumes direct replacement of primary vegetation within already cultivated landscapes and linear biodiversity responses, omitting fragmentation and edge effects that can amplify losses.
RCAR relies on GBIF-derived range sizes that may be biased by uneven sampling effort; bias corrections or alternative range sources are not explored beyond citing prior robustness.
Uncertainty propagation in scenario projections (e.g., parametric and data-layer uncertainty) is not quantified.
The rationale and implications of weighting by crop area fraction could be discussed more transparently (e.g., potential biases if sampling within “cropland” is not the focal crop).
The interpretation of RCAR changes could be clarified with examples and cross-checks against community similarity metrics to aid reader intuition.
More explicit guidance on the magnitude and spatial distribution of effects (e.g., maps with confidence intervals, partial dependence plots) would improve interpretability.

The study could more explicitly situate its findings relative to integrated bioeconomic and land-use models showing rebound/compensatory dynamics and demand-side leverage (e.g., Leclère et al. 2020; related systems modeling and ABM work).

Recent work on ecological intensification and landscape configuration (hedgerows/SNH connectivity) and their scale-dependent effects on biodiversity and services could be more directly connected to managerial implications.

Potential confounding by range size and habitat amount: range area is a strong predictor of extinction risk yet appears absent from the model; the included “proportion suitable” may not adequately control for total range extent.

The fragmentation metric (mean interior distance to edge) is strongly correlated with habitat amount and patch size; although “proportion suitable” and “patch isolation” are included, residual collinearity and scale dependence could bias variable importance.

Temporal alignment is unclear: fragmentation appears to be measured at a single or limited time slice while extinction risk transitions span 1996–2020; HFP baselines (2000/2018) and IUCN dates (1996/2020) are misaligned, risking attribution biases.

The claim that fragmentation outperforms habitat loss is insufficiently supported because direct measures of habitat loss (e.g., AOH/land-cover loss over time) do not appear as predictors; changes in HFP within suitable habitat are not equivalent to habitat loss.

The binary split of matrix quality at 50% high-HFP is arbitrary; although an interaction is modeled continuously (Fig. 3), robustness to other splits/thresholds (e.g., HFP ≥1, 4, 7, 10) is not assessed.
Unaddressed spatial and phylogenetic autocorrelation may inflate model performance and importance metrics; cross-validation that does not block by realm/region or phylogeny can overstate generality.
IUCN category changes can be non-genuine (taxonomy/knowledge/criteria revisions). There is no indication that these were filtered or modeled, which may contaminate the signal.

Methods detail for key computations (e.g., exact fragmentation computation, spatial resolution, weighting across patches, time points used for fragmentation/HFP) is insufficient in the excerpt; reproducibility would benefit from more explicit descriptions and code availability.
The choice and calculation of variable-importance metric (e.g., permutation vs Gini) and steps to mitigate bias from correlated predictors are not stated.

Climate change exposure (e.g., thermal stress variability, climate velocity) is not incorporated, despite its growing role in extinction risk; comparison to studies emphasizing climatic drivers would contextualize scope.
Alternative connectivity/fragmentation measures (graph-theoretic connectivity, resistance-based metrics using HFP or land cover, effective mesh size) are not discussed or tested.

No comparison with other recent extinction-risk modeling pipelines that integrate SDMs, land-use change, and human pressures (e.g., deep-SDM-based risk classifiers) to benchmark predictive power and interpretability.

Lack of detail on critical FL choices (e.g., exact aggregation weighting, straggler handling, participation variability per round) given severe client-size imbalance raises concerns about convergence dynamics and representation equity across sites.

Model design uses three independent sigmoid channels for nested labels (ET ⊂ TC ⊂ WT) without explicit structural constraints; potential inconsistencies and missed opportunities for topology-aware learning are not addressed.

Privacy is improved via TEE on the aggregator, but there is no analysis of client update leakage risk (e.g., gradient inversion, membership inference) or use of secure aggregation/differential privacy.

Comparisons are limited to the “public initial model”; there is no strong baseline such as (i) centralized training on any sizable shareable subset, (ii) state-of-the-art backbones (e.g., nnU-Net) retrained under comparable constraints, or (iii) alternative FL algorithms (e.g., FedProx, personalized FL, or DG-enhanced FL).

Ambiguity about annotation provenance and quality control: the methods mention label fusion and integration with multiple algorithms, but it is unclear when/where automated labels were used, how manual refinements were standardized, and whether inter-rater reliability was assessed across 71 sites.

Preprocessing details (e.g., intensity normalization, resampling strategy for 2D/3D, skull stripping failure handling) are not sufficiently specified to ensure reproducibility and to interpret domain-shift mitigation.

Single case study; reproducibility claims would be stronger with multiple pipelines or modalities and cross-institutional validation.

Use of Colab/GCP without providing containerized, pinned environments (e.g., Docker/Singularity) limits long-term determinism and portability.
Limited statistical characterization beyond AUC/KM p-values; absence of C-index, hazard ratios, or calibration assessment for survival analysis.

Lack of ablations on preprocessing choices to illustrate sensitivity and identify critical parameters.
Minimal reporting on computational resource use, runtimes, and monetary cost; readers cannot assess practical feasibility at scale.

Limited positioning relative to other cloud-native reproducibility efforts (e.g., acia-workflows, workflow systems like CWL/Nextflow, or containerized notebook platforms such as JupyterHub/Binder).
No substantive comparison with alternative infrastructures (on-prem/HPC vs cloud) or discussion of cost/performance trade-offs shown in recent studies.
Physical-time mapping in coarse-grained Langevin simulations is not rigorously justified; reported μs−1 “rates” may be sensitive to friction, timestep, and MC attempt frequency.
The MSM validation is demonstrated primarily for single-reactive-site systems; generalization to multi-site, multi-enzyme networks (with competing cycles) is not validated in the same depth.

Force-field specification and parameterization for pSer (charge state, short-range interactions) are not described in sufficient detail to assess transferability or to reproduce results.

Stoichiometries and absolute enzyme concentrations in the condensate simulations (1–5 kinases for 200 chains in a 100 nm box) may not map straightforwardly to physiological regimes; robustness to concentration, salt, and temperature is not explored.

Limited positioning against prior reactive/coarse-grained MD+MC approaches and other recent CG frameworks designed for IDPs or PTM handling.

The connection to broader theories of LLPS (e.g., RPA/sequencedependent models) and to machine-learned CGs is only implicit; a clearer comparison would help contextualize sequence effects and modeling choices.

Limited baselines: the primary comparison is to PG; contemporary learned baselines (e.g., graph-based polyGNN; more recent multimodal or transformer polymer models) are absent from the core evaluation.

Potential confound of copolymer handling is insufficiently documented (how are multiple monomers and compositions encoded for the predictor?).
Uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution detection are not provided, despite the intended use in large-scale screening and boundary estimation.
Key pretraining details (vocabulary size, max sequence length, model depth/width, training time and hardware) are not fully specified in the main text.

The precise data split protocol per property (by polymer or by record) is not spelled out, which is important for avoiding target leakage across closely related records.

Recent polymer foundation and multimodal models are not discussed (e.g., polyGNN, MMPolymer, polyBART, PolyLLMem) that provide alternative featurization and in some cases stronger accuracy on overlapping benchmarks.

Broader context from molecular-language models (e.g., ChemBERTa, large-scale frozen-embedding benchmarks) could inform the discussion on when learned text embeddings surpass classical fingerprints and when they do not.

Lack of direct terminal stimulation/inhibition tests to confirm that respiratory effects are mediated via medullary projections (e.g., pre-Bötzinger, CVLM).

Sex as a biological variable is not examined; all experiments are in males, limiting translational scope.
The hypothesized sensory feedback mechanism for arousal at ~240–250 bpm is not directly tested (e.g., via deafferentation or selective muscle EMG analysis).
CO2 kinetics in the chamber and arterial/blood CO2 validation are not reported; latency interpretations rely on inferred timing.
Some statistical reporting inconsistencies (e.g., typographical artifacts like “p = -0.027”) and occasional formatting issues from PDF extraction hinder precision.
Figures (as described) could benefit from standardized axis units, effect sizes, and confidence intervals to facilitate comparison across conditions.
Limited discussion of how PBFoxP2 fits with other brainstem chemosensory nodes (e.g., RTN/pFRG, raphe) in quantitative terms or causal hierarchy.
The recent literature on parabrachial modularity in homeostatic control (e.g., lineage/single-cell transcriptomics) could better contextualize FoxP2 as a marker versus functional identity.

All molecular and connectomic predictors are derived from healthy cohorts; disease- and age-specific alterations in these features are not modeled, potentially biasing inference about pathophysiological mechanisms.

Multicollinearity among molecular predictors (e.g., gene PC1, myelination, metabolism) complicates attribution in linear/dominance analyses; PC1 reductions may obscure receptor- or gene-specific effects.
The neighbor abnormality metric divides by degree while multiplying by SC weights; without normalization by the sum of weights, weighted averaging may be biased by degree heterogeneity.
Centrality definitions on weighted graphs can be sensitive to weight-to-length transformations; precise choices and robustness are not fully detailed.
Analyses are restricted to 68 DK parcels, precluding subcortex/cerebellum and limiting spatial resolution; receptor/transcriptomic maps may lose informative variance at this scale.
The ENIGMA-derived effect sizes integrate heterogeneous cohorts (medication, comorbidities, chronicity), but potential systematic confounds are not explicitly modeled.
Linear models may underfit non-linear or interaction effects among predictors; mediation and moderation between molecular vulnerability and network exposure are not formally tested.
Structural connectivity is from a single, modest sample (n=70) and a single tractography/reconstruction approach; generalization across connectome datasets is not shown.
Main-text emphasis is on in-sample adjusted R²; cross-validated performance and uncertainty (e.g., confidence/credible intervals) could be more prominent in the main figures.
Some choices (e.g., parameterization of centrality on weighted networks, normalization in exposure computations) are deferred to Methods and could benefit from added precision in the main text.

Mechanistic network-diffusion/convolution models of pathology spread (e.g., in AD) show sensitivity to graph operators and kernels; a brief contrast would contextualize the exposure findings and suggest extensions.
Recent multi-level association frameworks that identify dense multimodal subnetworks (e.g., MOAT) could provide complementary inference beyond per-region regressions.
“In-sensor adaptive machine learning” and “standalone” claims appear overstated: most ML processing is performed in the cloud; the on-patch MCU is not executing the CNN or on-device adaptation.
Potential safety and durability risks of Ag nanowires in hydrogels (e.g., ion release, long-term skin exposure) are not comprehensively characterized beyond short-term cell viability.
Limited discussion of antenna/body-channel detuning under real use, coexistence interference, and BLE link robustness under movement and sweat.

Small human cohort (training on 5 subjects, testing on 2), all apparently healthy; no clinical population data; limited assessment of day-to-day variability, re-attachment, or sensor placement shifts.

Limited longitudinal wear testing (hours–days), sweat/water exposure studies, hydration/dehydration cycles of hydrogel, and motion artifacts under real ambulatory conditions.

Claims of robustness to motion artifacts are not benchmarked against strong, recent flexible electrode baselines; SNR/PSD comparisons to a “commercial device” lack precise specification and standardized metrics.
Insufficient detail on the “2D-like sequential feature extractor” (exact tensorization procedure, architecture specifics, parameter counts), and on triplet loss configuration and sampling strategy.
The term “adaptive” is used to describe generalization to new subjects without explicit on-device or online adaptation; this can be misleading.
Return loss description (“< 10 dB”) is ambiguous; conventionally S11 < −10 dB indicates acceptable matching; signs/units should be explicit.

No systematic comparison to sequence models that explicitly handle temporal dependencies (e.g., LSTM/GRU, TCNs), or to simpler feature-based classifiers; no ablation of modality contributions (sEMG vs ACC vs fusion).
Limited discussion of on-device ML or model compression/pruning to enable true in-sensor inference compared to emerging wearable edge-AI platforms (e.g., BioGAP-Ultra).
Minimal connection to recent large-scale SSL/pretraining for wearables that could improve generalization (e.g., strategies akin to day-long context modeling with learned masking).
The electrochemical dissolution of gold generates AuCl4−; local ocular safety, cumulative gold ion exposure, and clearance are not quantified or discussed in depth.

Cross-sensitivities of the strain sensor to temperature, hydration, ocular biomechanics (e.g., corneal thickness, stiffness), and tear osmolarity are only partially addressed; TCR exists but impact on IOP accuracy is not modeled.
Long-term mechanical and electrical stability of the sensor/DDS/packaging in the tear environment (salt, proteins, lipids) and under blink-induced shear has not been demonstrated.
Oxygen permeability (Dk/t) and tear exchange in the presence of embedded films/passivation layers are not reported; chronic hypoxia risk remains unaddressed.
In vivo sample sizes, variance, and statistical testing details (n, error bars, blinding) are inconsistently reported; outcomes such as “22% IOP reduction” would benefit from full statistics.
Agreement with tonometry (R² = 0.88; LoA ≈ ±3 mmHg) is promising but not benchmarked against existing devices (e.g., Triggerfish, implantables); drift over days/weeks was not quantified.

Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics of timolol from the DDS (ocular tissue levels, aqueous humor concentrations, systemic exposure) are not measured; comparison with eye drops focuses on outcomes but lacks PK support.
Weekly-type DDS is proposed, but in vivo data appear limited to daily/every-other-day use; multi-dose reliability and inter-dose crosstalk are not fully explored on-eye.

Some fabrication parameters critical to reproducibility (e.g., exact Au shell thickness distribution, residual Ag quantification, PEDOT:PSS formulation and crosslinking details) are not fully specified.

Prior art on on-eye drug delivery (e.g., hydrogel-lens reservoirs, micro-reservoir MEMS, osmotic lenses) is not comprehensively discussed, especially safety/PK learnings relevant to this DDS.
Ambiguity of MS/MS-based attribution (e.g., isomers/stereoisomers, shared substructures) is inherent; reliance on cosine similarity without explicit FDR control can inflate false positives.

Instrumental heterogeneity (ion mode, collision energy, adducts) and media/background signals may affect match reliability; harmonization strategies are not described in depth.
Lacks quantitative benchmarking of precision/recall, false discovery rates (via decoys or permutation), or comparisons to MASST or fragment-centric alternatives for taxonomic inference.

Search parameter defaults (m/z tolerance, fragment tolerances, minimum matched peaks, score thresholds) and their impact on sensitivity/specificity are not quantitatively explored.

Toxic component contribution analysis assumes additivity and does not account for mixture interactions (synergy/antagonism).
Focuses on primary PM2.5; excludes secondary aerosol formation, which is substantial for power sector emissions and could alter control priorities if toxicity of secondary PM were incorporated.
Extraction conditions and high-temperature sampling (heated lines) can alter semi-volatile species and PAHs, potentially biasing toxicity estimates.
Representativeness of EAF-based steelmaking is limited by small sample size; conclusions about process-specific toxicity in ISI may thus be incomplete.
Use of 16 EPA priority PAHs omits many oxygenated/nitrated PAHs and other organics known to influence toxicity.
The definition of EC1.5 as “1.5-fold inhibition of ROS generation” is likely a wording error and needs clarification; dose metric choices and normalization could be better justified.
Uncertainty propagation through WRF-CMAQ (model structural and meteorological uncertainties) appears limited; only inventory/toxicity uncertainties are quantified for TPAE.
The reported percentage reductions in nationwide population-weighted PM2.5 exposure under sectoral ULE scenarios are ambiguous (relative to total ambient PM2.5 or sector-attributable portions).
The exact mapping from in vitro toxic units to TPAE scaling factors could be explained more explicitly, including units and normalization.
Figures referenced are essential for interpretation (e.g., spatial maps, Supplementary Tables), and key numerical results could be summarized in-text for self-containment.
Limited discussion of oxidative potential assays (e.g., DTT) and epidemiological literature linking source/chemical-specific metrics to health outcomes for triangulation.
More explicit comparison to prior toxicity-integrated policy frameworks (e.g., health-risk weighting in source apportionment, redox-active metal literature) would strengthen context.
Discussion could better situate how secondary sulfate/nitrate toxicity compares to primary metal-rich PM from industry, referencing recent toxicological/epidemiological findings.
Assumption of additivity/independence when summing temperature-attributable and COVID-19 deaths may not hold under interaction or shared etiologies; potential under/overcounting if risks interact.
DLNM fitted across 1981–2022 assumes stationarity of temperature–mortality relations; pandemic-era behavior, healthcare access, and pathogen ecology likely modified these associations.
COVID-19 removal based on death-certificate coding may miss indirect COVID-19 effects (deferred care, healthcare strain), potentially biasing attribution to temperature.
Limited Monte Carlo draws (n=100) for uncertainty propagation may understate interval variability.

Comparability of event definitions pre-2016 (proxy criteria) vs post-2016 (UKHSA alerts) may introduce ascertainment bias in decade comparisons; no sensitivity using unified percentile-based definitions over the full period.
No adjustment for co-exposures (e.g., air pollution, influenza/RSV), which can confound temperature–mortality associations, especially in winter.
Age aggregation may mask heterogeneous vulnerability; lack of age- or cause-specific stratification limits mechanistic insight and policy targeting.
Use of daily average of (Tmax+Tmin)/2 and admin-region averages may misclassify exposure; sensitivity to alternative metrics (UTCI, apparent temperature, humidity, wind, radiation) is not reported.
Ratios and fold-change comparisons are presented without confidence intervals, limiting inferential strength.
Interpretation of the +91 COVID deaths on 19 July 2022 as “exacerbation” by heat risks over-interpretation without a formal counterfactual.

Limited discussion of recent methodological integrations of DLNMs with stochastic mortality models and spatio-temporal frameworks that explicitly separate climate-driven risk and trend components (e.g., Li–Lee/DLNM coupling, mixed-frequency DLNMs, BYM2 spatial priors, penalized multi-region DLNMs).

The causal-inference literature on time-varying confounding and epidemic intervention assessment is pertinent to interpreting temperature–COVID interplay and could strengthen the discussion of limitations.

Methodological specifics are insufficient to fully assess soundness: the concentration–response functions (CRFs) used (IER vs GEMM vs MR-BRT), how uncertainty in CRFs and exposures was propagated, and how disease mortalities were projected to 2035 are not fully described.

The construction and validation of PM2.5 fields from CMIP6 are unclear (model selection, ensemble strategy, bias correction/downscaling, comparison to observation-based surfaces), raising concerns about exposure accuracy at provincial scale.
Decomposition method details are sparse (e.g., LMDI vs Shapley vs other), making it hard to judge how interaction terms were handled and whether attribution is path-independent and fair.
Limited validation of historical DAPP against independent benchmarks (e.g., GBD/State of Global Air) at provincial level, and no multi-dataset robustness (satellite/CTM exposure products).
No sensitivity analysis to alternative CRFs (e.g., GEMM 2019/2022 vs legacy IER), which can materially change DAPP levels and trends.
It is unclear how age-standardized disease mortalities were extrapolated under each SSP; the linkage to SSP health-system trajectories and potential endogeneity with air quality is not specified.

Scenario labels and units appear inconsistent in places (e.g., “SSP3-7.5” vs “SSP3-7.0”; “ug/cm³” instead of µg/m³; “blood heart disease”). Some numerical repetition in waterfall plots suggests possible templating or transcription artifacts.
Per-capita DAPP phrasing is sometimes confusing (e.g., “855 people (per 10,000 people)”); ensure consistent units and denominators.

Limited engagement with recent mortality forecasting advances and age-structure metrics that can contextualize aging effects (e.g., flow-field mortality forecasting, population-pyramid–linked metrics), and with recent CRF developments (GEMM).

While the paper cites gaps in prior Chinese studies, it would benefit from a more systematic comparison to recent provincial or multi-driver studies and to exposure modeling work using joint mean-extreme frameworks or finer-scale data.
The identifiability of NMF factors in this setting is not fully characterized; demixing may fail with spatially similar fingerprints or temporally correlated sources—common in neural circuits.
The approach relies on stability of fingerprints over time and against perturbations (fiber bending, temperature, micromotion), which are not assessed experimentally.
The method’s performance bounds (e.g., maximum resolvable sources vs. SNR and fingerprint coherence) are not quantified.
Validation is limited to in vitro conditions with DMD-imposed ground truth and fixed tissue; no in vivo data, motion, or hemodynamics are tested.
Rank selection is handled manually; there is no robust, data-driven criterion or stability analysis to prevent over/under-factorization.
The miniscope experiments demonstrate sensitivity to single-source fingerprints but do not yet demonstrate demixing of multiple simultaneous sources using the miniscope.
The term “unconstrained NMF” is potentially confusing given that non-negativity is itself a constraint; also, l1_ratio is set but with zero alphas (thus inactive), which could be clarified.
Quantitative performance metrics focus on trace correlations; additional assessments (e.g., event detection accuracy, crosstalk matrices, residual analyses) would give a fuller picture.
Comparison to CNMF/CNMF-E approaches used in microendoscopy for demixing calcium signals could be deepened, including a baseline comparison on the same datasets.
While prior MMF imaging and learning-based reconstructions are cited, explicit discussion of conditions under which NMF would outperform or fail relative to learned approaches is limited.

The “constant-time” and energy claims omit critical system components (laser sources, detectors/ADCs, interconnects, repeat passes for multiple layers), potentially overstating practical throughput and underestimating power.
The demonstrated experiment validates only a DONN kernel, not the full ONE stack (including XBAR and nonlinear stages), leaving system-level feasibility and integration challenges unaddressed.
Nonlinear operations are electronic; the cumulative opto-electronic conversion overhead, latencies, and synchronization are not modeled in end-to-end performance estimates.

Reported comparisons emphasize training/validation loss rather than standardized test metrics (e.g., relative L2, nRMSE) with error bars and multiple random seeds; some figures compare losses across models without equalized training protocols, which may limit fairness.
There is limited ablation to isolate the contributions of the Fourier branch, real-space branch, and physics-parameter conditioning.
Generalization properties central to operator learning (cross-resolution, geometry variation, boundary-condition shifts, temporal extrapolation) are not systematically evaluated.
Error definitions and scales vary across tasks (absolute, normalized, relative), making cross-task comparisons hard; a unified metric suite would help.

Data generation details (boundary conditions, coefficient distributions, solver discretizations, time-stepping choices) are insufficient for exact reproducibility or for assessing distribution shift robustness.

The discussion of neural-operator baselines is incomplete relative to recent spectral/multiscale/attentional advances (e.g., hierarchical attentive FNOs, DPNO, NSM). Stronger baselines and discussion are warranted, especially for multiscale and time-dependent problems.

Related “O(1)-in-time” neural surrogates conditioned on timestep and parameters (e.g., time-conditioned EM surrogates) are relevant to the constant-time narrative and could better contextualize ONE’s claims.
The self-supervised update with pseudo-labels risks confirmation bias and error accumulation; formal safeguards, error detectors, or theoretical guarantees are not provided.
Confidence weighting appears internally inconsistent: the provided formula seems to up-weight low-confidence experts; the definition of “confidence” may also be flawed (see detailed comments).
Scalability to higher spatial DoF, grayscale inputs, or phase-sensitive scenarios is not demonstrated; experiments focus on binary 16×16 and 32×32 patterns.

Comparisons are limited primarily to a single StaticNN baseline; missing evaluations against other adaptive strategies (e.g., periodic TM/RVITM refresh, vectorial time reversal refresh, configuration training, dynamic synthesis networks, continual-learning baselines).
Ablations are sparse: no systematic study of update interval, forgetting schedule, router/gating alternatives, or sensitivity to pseudo-label noise is provided.
Update-time latency and compute budget per 5 s batch are not reported, leaving unclear whether the system is truly real-time in practice.
The confidence metric and weighting equations appear contradictory or erroneous (details below).
The “rebuild/copy” schedule for short-term experts is under-specified (what is copied, from which expert, and with what initialization?).
The video compression ratio is reported as 1.39‰, which is unconventional and hard to interpret without bitrate/throughput context.
Limited engagement with recent adaptive or physics-driven dynamic compensation methods (e.g., time-averaged TM/fluctuation eigenchannels, adjoint optimization in dynamic media).
The relationship to (and potential complementarity with) RVITM-type fast intensity-only characterization and SmoothGS single-iteration TM recovery is not experimentally explored.

Reliance on the local-phase (locally periodic) approximation and RCWA unit-cell modeling leaves inter-cell coupling and high-NA effects unaccounted for; this can reduce predictive fidelity for NA≈0.45.
The computational backend uses an INR-based semi-blind deconvolution, which is comparatively heavy-weight despite being termed “simple”; real-time feasibility and robustness are not quantified.
The design objective samples only two incident angles (0° and 10°); FOV performance and angular aberration control are not comprehensively addressed.
Quantitative metrics such as measured MTFs across wavelengths/field angles, focusing/transmission efficiencies, and SNR/throughput are sparse in the main text.
Fairness and parity of the computational reconstruction across different optics (same priors/hyperparameters/initialization) are not fully detailed; this matters for comparing image quality.
PSF measurements are confined to 8.23–10.93 μm; 12 μm behavior is inferred via filtered imaging but not directly measured with the same PSF protocol.

Several inconsistencies in reported device parameters and sampling: period Λ=4 μm vs. Λ=10 μm; aperture 1 cm vs. statements implying 2.5 cm or 10 cm; “403 × 101” RCWA simulations appears to be 40^3 × 101; “8 optimized wavelengths” vs. “13 wavelengths during optimization.” These should be reconciled.
The term “simple computational backend” understates the sophistication of the INR deconvolution; clarify terminology.

Limited discussion of closely related hybrid optical-computational LWIR efforts (e.g., hybrid meta-refractive correction), multiwavelength multilayer metasurfaces, and prior visible-band inverse-designed EDOF metasurfaces that use similar multi-scale differentiable pipelines.
No baseline comparison with forward EDOF masks (e.g., cubic/log-asphere) in LWIR, or with MDLs that have shown broadband LWIR imaging.

Reliance on the point-dipole model (PDM) to invert near-field signals into dielectric function and radiative rates introduces model dependence; sensitivity to tip geometry, tapping amplitude, and tip–sample distance is not fully quantified.
The Lorentzian parametrization conflates dephasing and nonradiative channels; the identifiability of radiative rate versus εbg and thickness d is not rigorously analyzed.
The screening length is concluded to be <20 nm but limited by spatial resolution; no deconvolution or tip-spread function analysis is attempted to refine this bound.
Twist-angle determination via SHG leaves a 30° ambiguity (15° vs 45°), and potential contributions from local strain or doping to the observed redshifts are not systematically excluded.
Parameter maps (ω0, γ, εbg) across the flakes are not shown, despite the capability of hyperspectral s-SNOM to reveal spatial inhomogeneity.

Notation in the Lorentzian model and Table 1 contains minor inconsistencies/typos (e.g., symbols for rates “Yr,o”, “Ynr+Yd”) that could confuse readers; εbg values and their physical meaning could be better contextualized.
The connection between phase contrast and absorption is cited but would benefit from a brief intuitive explanation tailored to the s-SNOM observable used.

Quantitative inversion approaches and harmonic-depth sensitivity analyses in visible s-SNOM (e.g., dual-harmonic inversion/inference methods) are not discussed; comparison to complementary far-field ellipsometry or reflectance on similar flakes is missing.
Recent near-field works on exciton–plasmon polaritons and cryogenic s-SNOM resolving negative ε1 regions provide useful context for the damping-limited room-temperature regime discussed here.
Key performance metrics (NEP, specific detectivity D*, noise spectra, response time/bandwidth, dynamic range, linearity) are not reported, limiting assessment against state-of-the-art.
Stability and retention of the ferroelectric domain pattern under device operation (temperature, humidity, optical/thermal cycling) are not quantified.
Angular/polarization dependence and tolerance of the plasmonic resonance are not characterized; incident angle sensitivity could impact practical imaging.
Uniformity, yield, and variability across pixels/channels are not addressed; nanoscale domain width control and its spread are critical for arrays.
The imaging results are simulated from commercial camera data rather than produced by a physically integrated multichannel array with on-chip readout, weakening system-level claims.
The relation between Raman G-band shifts and EF is treated simplistically; potential confounds from strain/temperature are not fully disentangled or calibrated.
The attribution of channel selectivity solely to plasmonic coupling would benefit from polarization controls, thermal background subtraction, and mechanism isolation (e.g., PTE vs PV vs bolometric).
The description of the transmission measurement using an AFM probe is unconventional and under-explained, raising questions about spot size, alignment, and sampling uniformity.
The “6-channel-pixel” physical layout and how six domain-widths are co-located within one pixel are not fully clarified; implications for fill factor and optical crosstalk are unclear.
Benchmarks against leading room-temperature MIR detectors (e.g., vdW b-AsP heterojunctions) in terms of D*, NEP, and speed are absent, despite comparable reported responsivities.
Comparison against prior graphene plasmonic detectors (nanopatterned, grating-coupled, or substrate-patterned) lacks a quantitative head-to-head with noise, uniformity, and scalability metrics.
The deep-learning imaging gains are not contrasted with software-only baselines (e.g., edge-preserving filters or multi-scale CNNs) on the same single-channel inputs.
Analogue assignment relies on expert judgment and heterogeneous criteria, risking circularity and sampling bias; no sensitivity analysis shows robustness to alternative analogue definitions.

The landmarking protocol emphasizes canal and cochlear centrelines; cross-sectional canal thickness and absolute canal size—key functional variables—are not directly captured after Procrustes scaling, yet are discussed in interpretations.
PLS dimension 4 has a non-significant p-value (≈0.10); interpretations should be clearly qualified or supported with additional evidence.
The inference that developmental/genetic complexity causes higher evolvability is largely speculative and not directly tested.
Limited intraspecific sampling (appears to be single or very few specimens per species) may conflate species means with individual variation and measurement error.

Allometry and body size effects are handled indirectly (via a context variable); a formal size-correction pipeline (e.g., regressing shape on centroid size and/or body mass with/without phylogeny) is not presented.
Convergence assessment is primarily distance-based; it would benefit from established phylogenetic convergence tests (e.g., Stayton’s C1–C5, Wheatsheaf index, SURFACE/l1ou).
Coding of ecological variables (e.g., “agility,” “3D movement”) appears ordinal/subjective; no inter-rater reliability or sensitivity analyses are shown.

Precise details of CT resolution, segmentation protocol, sliding criteria for semilandmarks, and measurement repeatability are not fully described here; reproducibility would benefit from explicit reporting.
Terminology occasionally implies absolute size (“smaller canals”) while the configuration captures scale-free geometry; wording should be aligned with what the data capture.

Work on rapid vestibular shape shifts and plasticity in captive versus wild Mus musculus (e.g., the 2024 study summarized in the related work) is not discussed; it bears on the timing of inner-ear development and potential plastic contributions to interspecific patterns.

More explicit contrasts with univariate canal radius-of-curvature scaling studies and hearing-range datasets could triangulate functional interpretations of cochlear coiling and vestibular morphology.

The use of a single trophic enrichment factor (3.4‰) and a single moose δ15N baseline (from 2014 samples) to derive trophic position across 1993–2016 and across space may introduce unmodeled baseline/TEF uncertainty and spatiotemporal bias.

Maternal learning is proxied by the mother’s posterior mean trophic position (initially across years), which risks temporal misalignment with the actual rearing period and statistical “shrinkage” that could bias effect sizes; although a reduced analysis with observed rearing-year maternal values was included, this is not the main model.

Potential collinearity and identifiability challenges between maternal learning (fixed effect of maternal phenotype), maternal effects (mother ID random effect), and environmental similarity are acknowledged but could still bias variance partitioning.

The pedigree (16 microsatellites) and sample size (71 daughters, 33 mothers) may limit power to detect additive genetic variance; the “negligible heritability” conclusion should be tempered accordingly.

Environmental similarity is reduced to a Euclidean distance in a space of broad habitat composition variables with equal weights; key resource covariates (e.g., local moose density/harvest remains, ant abundance proxies, berry productivity) are not modeled directly, potentially underestimating environmental effects.

Year-specific diet samples are paired with a single home range composition per individual (median year used when multiple years are available), which may decouple diet and environment for repeated measures.

δ15N-based trophic position collapses dietary space into a single axis without accounting for multi-source mixing or routing; ants and moose having similar δ15N complicates interpretation of “carnivory” vs. insectivory.
The reported credible interval for the environmental component “9% [0.1–5%]” appears internally inconsistent (upper bound < point estimate), suggesting a reporting error.
Minor internal inconsistencies (e.g., environmental contribution sometimes 12%, sometimes 9%) and the questionable CI undermine interpretability.
The phrase “half a trophic position” for a range of 2.7–3.1 (≈0.4) is imprecise and should be reported exactly.
Work on stable isotope mixing models and compound-specific amino acid δ15N for improved trophic resolution is not discussed; these methods could address baseline and routing concerns.
A broader quantitative genetics context on the power and identifiability constraints of animal models in spatially structured pedigrees could strengthen the interpretation of low heritability.
Reliance on PROSAIL inversion for LAI and ALA without explicit uncertainty quantification; LAI saturation >4–5 and canopy clumping effects may bias estimates.

Stomatal conductance is validated indoors (gas exchange vs Penman–Monteith inversion) but lacks any form of field-level validation or surrogate (e.g., calibrated thermal imaging under controlled conditions).
Environmental translation of leaf width/length is demonstrated on a single hybrid for the environmental-response regressions; genotype-specific response heterogeneity is not explored.
Genomic prediction is limited to main-effect G-BLUP; no explicit G×E reaction-norm modeling that leverages environmental covariates to predict environment-specific trait values.
External validation sample sizes are limited for some traits (e.g., architecture on 20 recent hybrids), and some external validations show modest effect sizes (e.g., ALA vs predicted rhPAD).
The link from adaptive trait predictions to downstream agronomic outcomes (e.g., yield stability, water-use efficiency) is not quantitatively demonstrated.
Details on field spatial correction, UAV radiometric/BRDF corrections, and PROSAIL configuration ranges are not presented in this excerpt, limiting assessment of measurement rigor.
Methods for deriving BLUEs/BLUPs, spatial modeling of field heterogeneity, and cross-validation stratification to prevent relatedness leakage are insufficiently detailed in the text provided.
The crop model inputs and parameterization (Lacube et al. 2020) could be more fully documented, including sensitivity to input errors and uncertainty propagation.

Recent advances in probabilistic/physics-informed inversions of PROSAIL that report uncertainty (e.g., GP-based or VAE-based decoders) are not discussed; these could strengthen claims surrounding UAV-based trait retrieval reliability.
Broader connections to distribution shift methodology (e.g., WILDS-style evaluation thinking) are relevant given the indoor→field and field→field translations, but not leveraged.
Opportunities to benchmark or validate architecture retrieval with emerging 3D field pipelines (e.g., TLS datasets or 3D Gaussian Splatting + segmentation) are not explored.
Multi-allelic modeling is fixed to k=2 for diploid genomes, which may not capture more complex copy-number allelic series or true triallelic heterozygous events in repetitive regions.
Genotyping is based on simple read-count ratios, which may underperform in low-complexity/repetitive regions or under variable coverage, and may not handle subclonality in tumors.

The local assembly module filters insertions <1 kb by design; while reasonable (since smaller insertions may be spanned), this could miss structurally complex but shorter events not well captured by read alignments.
Limited stratified benchmarking in segmental duplications, VNTRs, and low-complexity regions where long-read SV calling is most error-prone and where most errors tend to concentrate.

Assembly-based callsets are treated as ground truth without extensive orthogonal validation (e.g., optical mapping, long-range PCR) for discrepant calls (especially enriched near telomeres/centromeres).
Tumor evaluation is limited to a single cell line without matched-normal analysis; the “tumor mode” criteria and performance for subclonal SVs are under-specified.

Some parameter rationales (e.g., N_supp = Depth/10 + 2) and algorithmic choices (density computation details, thresholds for clustering peaks) would benefit from deeper justification and sensitivity analyses.
The extent to which pbsv was run under recommended aligners (pbmm2) and the platform-appropriateness of each comparator is not always clearly stated.

Comparisons to other long-read SV tools such as SVIM (and newer versions like Sniffles2, SVDSS, or longcallD) are not presented; related work on haplotype-aware realignment or reassembly-based refinement in repeats could better contextualize claims.
Limited discussion of pangenome/graph-based approaches and T2T references that may reduce reference-bias at challenging loci.
Reliance on 151-bp short reads limits accurate genotyping of longer repeats; callability drops for RRT length > ~80 bp, potentially biasing rate and spectrum estimates.
Only ~40% of STRs passed trio-level QC for mDNM testing; implications for false negative rates and extrapolation to genome-wide burdens are not fully quantified.
Homopolymers, a substantial and biologically important class, carry higher error rates; while sensitivity analyses help, residual systematic biases may remain.
The mDNM GWAS is confined to Icelandic trios; no independent replication cohort of trios is presented for the genetic associations.
Unclear whether per-trio callability (number of testable STRs) is explicitly modeled as an offset/denominator in the GWAS phenotype to avoid technical confounding.
Limited functional follow-up for the NEIL2 synonymous variant; mechanistic plausibility is discussed but direct evidence (eQTL/splicing, protein impact) is not provided.
Parent-of-origin assigned for 60% of events; potential biases in the remaining 40% unassigned fraction are not extensively explored.
Occasional formatting artifacts (e.g., stray numerals near SNP IDs) and incomplete details relegated to Supplementary materials may hinder full reproducibility from the main text.
The exact regression framework for age effects and GWAS (e.g., Poisson/negative binomial vs. linear on standardized residuals) could be stated more explicitly.
A more direct comparison to recent genome-wide tandem repeat DNM studies (e.g., Mitra et al., 2021, autism-focused) would help situate the magnitude and spectrum differences.
Discussion of state-of-the-art STR mutation process models and stutter-correction frameworks could further contextualize limitations of short-read calling at homopolymers.

The practical HSR detection rule (uncut alignments with ≥3 differences) only approximates the formal HSR-score definition and may depend heavily on aligner scoring schemes and reference divergence; robustness to mapper choice/parameters is not thoroughly explored.
Potential confounding of HSR evidence by local SNP/indel density, low-complexity regions, and platform-specific error profiles is discussed qualitatively but lacks dedicated quantitative controls.
The method focuses on single-copy tandem duplications and deletions; support for multi-copy gains, complex or nested events, and interspersed duplications remains unclear.
Limited ablation studies: the incremental contributions of HSRs, insert-size statistics, depth filters, and the random forest model are not decomposed quantitatively.
Breakpoint precision is claimed as a strength, but a formal, size-stratified breakpoint accuracy comparison (e.g., within 1–5 bp) vs. baselines is not reported.

Generalization across sequencing settings (read length, insert-size distributions, lower coverage, PCR vs PCR-free) is only partially addressed; performance sensitivity to these parameters would be valuable.
The mapping from the formal HSR-score to the practical heuristic (≥3 mismatches/indels) could be clarified with calibration curves and thresholds per aligner.
Details of the junction realignment step, overlap-extension, and pairing heuristics could use more algorithmic specificity and complexity analysis.

While the chosen baselines align with common practice and prior benchmarks, recent high-performing short-read SV callers (e.g., GRIDSS2, SvABA, Wham, TIDDIT, CNVnator for depth-only baselines) are not included; a brief rationale or subset comparisons would strengthen positioning.

Discussion could better situate the work relative to LUMPY’s probabilistic breakpoint integration framework and to population-scale tandem-duplication surveys in model organisms that reported limits of split-read approaches in repeats.

The pull-down from tissue lysates may capture rare or transient complexes but does not quantify endogenous copy numbers; causality between specific off-target peptides and observed tissue killing remains indirect without peptide-level abundance confirmation in the same model.
Reliance on peptide pulsing (T2 assays) to demonstrate functional recognition does not ensure that endogenously processed/presented levels are sufficient to drive physiological toxicity.
The framework’s sensitivity and detection limits are not characterized (e.g., minimal copies per cell detectable, FDR for peptide IDs in the enrichment context).
Number of human tissue donors, HLA genotypes, and donor-to-donor variability are not explicitly reported; allele matching (HLA-A*02:01) is essential for interpreting specificity and generalizability.
Lack of targeted quantification (e.g., PRM/SRM) of the identified off-target peptides in liver (or spheroids) to link presence and abundance to observed ESK1-mediated killing.
No orthogonal validation of peptide–ESK1 binding kinetics/affinity (e.g., SPR with refolded pHLA), especially for peptides eliciting stronger activation than the WT1 index peptide.
Structural modeling provides plausible binding modes, but no accompanying mutational or energetic measurements to confirm the proposed compensation motif.
Minor inconsistencies (e.g., reported length of the shortened MAGE-A4 peptide; occasional 2D vs 3D wording for spheroids) could confuse readers and should be clarified.
Statistical treatment of interactome enrichment (replicates, FDR control, criteria for “significant enrichment”) is referenced but not detailed in the provided text.

The claim of “first” experimental platform would benefit from tighter contextualization against prior reverse immunology or soluble TCR-based IP approaches, targeted immunopeptidomics with pHLA-specific binders, and recent structure-/AI-based cross-reactivity predictors.

Integration with contemporary computational approaches (e.g., structure-guided scoring/design such as HERMES; sequence-based peptide-agnostic predictors such as DapPep; broader ML/TCR modeling and reinforcement-learning optimization) is not explored, limiting the cross-disciplinary impact.
Dependence on specific substrate architecture (pyridine-alkyne eneyne tethers and, for α-C–C cleavage, a cyclopropyl bridge) may limit generality.

Proposed 8π electrocyclization and “tricyclic metal-carbene” intermediacy, while plausible, lack direct experimental or computational corroboration (e.g., no carbene trapping, spectroscopy, or DFT analysis).
Reaction temperatures are relatively high and, for the α-C–C cleavage, require CHCl3 and a silver salt with a phase-transfer agent; sustainability and cost could be concerns.
The origin and control of diastereoselectivity/stereochemical outcomes are not deeply analyzed.
Functional group tolerance for strongly coordinating, protic, or redox-sensitive moieties (free amines, aldehydes, acids, nitro groups) is insufficiently explored or documented.
The α-C–C cleavage manifold is mostly limited to cyclopropanes; other strained motifs (cyclobutanes, vinylcyclopropanes, donor–acceptor cyclopropanes) are not examined.
Limited kinetics, mechanistic rate studies, or competition experiments; no KIE data for α-C–H cleavage; no Hammett analysis to probe electronic effects.
The role of water/protons in the two protonation events is inferred but not definitively established (e.g., water content control, molecular sieves, alternative proton sources).
Some nomenclature and abbreviations (e.g., CuTc vs CuTC, TEBA) could be standardized/defined on first use; a few grammatical and formatting inconsistencies remain.
The mechanistic figure would benefit from explicit metal oxidation states/ligands and clearer bookkeeping of charges and protonation steps.
Tables are referenced but not shown in the main text excerpt; clarity about yields, selectivity, and conditions should be consolidated.

While the paper cites foundational literature on enyne cycloisomerizations, carbenes, and 8π electrocyclizations, it could better contextualize against recent advances in: (i) gold/copper-catalyzed formation and reactivity of vinyl metal zwitterions in N-fused systems; (ii) medium-ring construction via electrocyclizations or sigmatropic rearrangements; (iii) ring-opening chemistry of cyclopropylcarbinyl cations under transition-metal catalysis.
Preliminary biological or physicochemical characterization (beyond synthetic access) of the new NCPC scaffold is not provided, which would strengthen the significance claims for medicinal chemistry.
Lack of quantitative electrochemical metrics (e.g., electrode potentials, faradaic efficiency, current–time/potential–time profiles) limits assessment of energy efficiency and scalability.
Undivided-cell operation in HF-rich media raises questions about cathodic processes, gas evolution, and potential competitive reactions that are not characterized.
The influence of mass transport and cell geometry on selectivity and rate is not discussed, though such factors can be decisive in anodic radical-cation chemistry.
No kinetic data, rate laws, or competition experiments to substantiate the claimed kinetic selectivity (MeOH vs Et3N·3HF) or the stepwise radical-to-carbocation sequence.
Limited stereochemical analysis for disubstituted/tri-substituted cyclopropanes; mechanistic stereochemical implications of three-electron SN2 opening are underexplored.
Oxyfluorination with ethers invokes oxonium intermediates; more direct evidence (e.g., 18O labeling, interception studies) would solidify this mechanistic branch.
Some yields are reported as GC/NMR without consistent isolated yields across the board, making cross-comparison harder.
Minor inconsistencies in reaction times and scales between entries and figures could be clarified to help reproducibility assessment.

A more explicit, side-by-side comparison with leading hypervalent iodine and photoredox methods for 1,3-difunctionalization (scope breadth, functional-group tolerance, scalability, cost, and safety) would better position the contribution.
Discussion of alternative mechanistic possibilities (e.g., direct fluorination pathways, chain processes) is relatively brief given the complexity of fluorination under electrochemical conditions.
Selectivity profiling is limited to two PLA2 comparators; broader off-target profiling (COX/LOX enzyme panels, kinases, receptors, transporters) is not reported.
The thiazolyl ketone warhead may present covalency/chemical reactivity concerns; glutathione adduction and thiol-reactivity data are lacking.
Plasma stability is reported, but solubility, permeability, metabolic stability (microsomes/S9), and CYP/hERG liabilities are not disclosed.

The mechanistic claim of PRC2-dependent transcriptional repression and ROS-mediated lethality is primarily correlative within the provided text; direct epigenetic and genetic validation is not shown here (e.g., H3K27me3 ChIP-seq, EZH2 dependency, PLA2G4A genetic perturbation).
Limited in vivo efficacy/PK-PD data: no leukemia models, tumor eicosanoid biomarker modulation, or tolerability data are provided.
Cell line screen size (n=66) is modest and may underpower genetic association analyses; multiple testing correction details and validation on independent cohorts are not fully described.
Table 1 “Human plasma stability” column uses unclear units/notations (e.g., “x”, “*”, “ND¤”) without in-text footnote definitions; timepoints differ (20–25 h) without rationale.
Diastereomeric/stereochemical issues for α-methyl analogs are not discussed; activity may be enantiomer-dependent.
The relation between XI(50) values and cellular IC50s needs clearer discussion of interfacial assay conditions and translation to cell systems.

Limited comparison with other recent small-molecule cPLA2α inhibitors beyond legacy references; benchmarking against state-of-the-art tool compounds across standardized biochemical and cellular assays would strengthen claims.
Prior reports linking PLA2G4A to epigenetic regulation or ROS homeostasis are not synthesized; the novelty claim would benefit from deeper contextualization and explicit contrasts.

Dependence on Assumption 0.2 (small noise-to-signal ratio) is strong for microbiome data where technical and sampling noise can be substantial; practical diagnostics or robustness analyses are not provided.

Handling of zeros conflates structural and sampling zeros—log-transformation is applied only when Mij=1, but in real data Mij is unknown; the resulting pairwise-complete approach may induce bias for rare taxa.

Distance correlation is unsigned; the recommendation to “borrow” the sign from linear correlation may be unstable in small n or weakly monotone nonlinear regimes; lack of a principled signed nonlinear dependence measure.
The cross-ecosystem “scale invariance” claim is asserted but not fully formalized; conditions for identifiability and comparability of Cj across ecosystems are not rigorously discussed.
Nonlinear baselines such as HSIC, MIC/MICe, or signed-kernel/energy-based measures are not included; this weakens claims of superiority for nonlinear detection.
P-value filtering is used without family-wise/FDR control; multiple-testing calibration is essential in network inference, especially with small n.
Simulation details on how differential sequencing efficiencies and sampling fractions are generated and estimated are deferred, limiting reproducibility of the bias-correction validation.
No sensitivity analyses for violations of assumptions (e.g., degree of noise, zero-inflation rates, co-occurrence prevalence thresholds, or misestimation of S and C).
Estimation of variances for the weighting scheme wj and practical computation in the presence of many zeros are not fully specified; guidance on robust estimation would help.
The computational complexity of distance correlation and strategies to scale to larger n (e.g., O(n log n) algorithms) are not discussed.
Closely related structural-zero covariance/precision estimation under pairwise-complete strategies (e.g., Kaul et al., 2016) is not cited, though the setup is similar.
Modern nonlinear dependence and energy/kernel-based methods (HSIC; fast unbiased dCor estimators) are not discussed; fast dCor computation (Huo & Székely, 2014) is relevant for scalability.

The model relies on simplified impedance elements (ideal capacitors) and neglects parasitic capacitances, Faradaic/leakage pathways, and diffusion-related Warburg/CPE behavior known to be relevant in physiological EIS.

The current-splitting factor f_OECT is treated as an empirical fit parameter, which weakens predictive power; its dependence on geometry and bias is acknowledged but not independently measured or modeled.
The electrolyte impedance Z_el is treated at a macroscopic level; potential frequency dispersion of the medium and non-ideal double layers are not explicitly included.
No quantitative noise spectra or SNR improvements are reported, despite the central motivation of gain for improving measurement fidelity.
Validation is limited to one cell line and a single electrolyte; broader exploration of media conductivity, ionic strength, or temperature dependence is absent.

The microparticle model captures geometric current constriction but omits membrane capacitance/seal resistance effects characteristic of cells; additional validation linking microparticle- and cell-induced impedance pathways would strengthen the analogy.
Limited statistics on device-to-device and cell-to-cell variability; the reported gain is compelling but its robustness across batches and conditions is not fully quantified.

Some symbols/assumptions (e.g., the exact derivation of VG* and its dependence on Z_el and Z_ch, and the mapping from microparticle distance to ΔZ_el via the proportionality p) could be detailed more thoroughly or supported by simulations.
The choice and extraction of Z_el from microelectrode fits is only briefly referenced; reporting the equivalent circuit used and fit quality would aid reproducibility.

The analysis would benefit from connecting to cell–substrate impedance models that explicitly treat finite/small electrodes relative to cell size (e.g., analytical treatments akin to Shiozawa & Uno, 2022), to position the microparticle model within single-cell EIS theory.

Diffusive/Warburg-like extracellular effects observed in biological media (e.g., non-ohmic frequency dependence) are not discussed; incorporating or bounding such effects would clarify applicability across preparations.
The results could be contextualized with recent high-gm electrolyte-gated transistor architectures (e.g., vertical nanogap EGTs) that may further increase gain within the same framework.

The central enabling mechanism—hard gate-oxide breakdown—raises reliability, repeatability, and long-term stability questions that are only partially addressed; the device degrades by ~25% after ~10^5 cycles and is “safe” only below ~7 mA.

The external quantum efficiency of the localized spot is extremely low (~1.4×10^-8 at 6 mA), and the total optical power reported for the spot (~94 pW) is very small, limiting immediate practical utility despite high spatial intensity.

The current density estimate uses the STI opening area as a proxy; the true recombination area shrinks with bias, so the actual current density in the active region is likely higher and is not precisely determined.
Lack of statistical data on device-to-device variability, wafer-scale yield, breakdown formation distributions (time-to-breakdown, voltage), and uniformity of emission area/power.

Thermal claims (no significant lattice heating) are inferred indirectly from spectral peak stability; direct thermal measurements or calibrated electro-thermal simulations would strengthen the conclusion.

Spatial coherence is asserted based on the in-line holography result, but not quantified (e.g., fringe visibility vs baseline, Young’s double-slit) or accompanied by coherence-length estimates given the broad spectrum (150–190 nm FWHM).
The “spatial intensity” metric is non-standard; radiance/brightness (W·sr^-1·m^-2) and total external efficiency are not provided, complicating fair comparison to prior work.
The methodology for absolute power calibration and error propagation (beyond PSF) is briefly referenced to the supplement; more detail in the main text would improve reproducibility.
The SMF-coupling measurement geometry is not fully specified (collection NA, alignment tolerance, fiber specifics versus emission spectrum), making the high 40–45% figure hard to interpret.
The holography section lacks exposure time, optical power on the sensor, and quantitative SNR metrics, which are important to assess practical viability.

Limited discussion of other CMOS-compatible Si emitters (e.g., W-center/defect centers in Si, dislocation-related emitters, MOS tunnel electroluminescence, Si avalanche EL in junctions/pillars), and Ge-on-Si or rare-earth emitters in CMOS contexts.
The promised benchmarking (supplementary S5) would be valuable as a concise table in the main text, using standardized metrics.

Reported PLED lifetimes (e.g., T70 ≈ 11.3 h for ultraflexible devices; other places T50 ≈ 41.5 h under different stress) are still limited for “long-term” monitoring and show inconsistencies in lifetime metrics and stress conditions.
Mechanical durability tests are short (50 cycles for PLED at 5 mm radius; 150 for OPD) and do not capture real-world strain scenarios (thousands of cycles, smaller radii, twisting).
Non-diode behavior attributed to ZnO roughness is noted but not deeply characterized or mitigated; this may affect power efficiency and reliability.
PPG demonstrated over short windows (7–20 s) with noticeable noise in ultraflexible operation; no multi-hour continuous monitoring or real-world activity tests are shown.
Lack of quantitative OPD noise metrics (dark current density vs bias, NEP, specific detectivity D*, linear dynamic range) that are standard in photodetector reporting.
OPV indoor-light performance and the self-powered operation at 1000 lux are argued from prior data and estimates but not experimentally demonstrated in the full system.
Limited statistical reporting (number of devices, variability, error bars) and no discussion of device yield or reproducibility.

Confusion between lifetime definitions and stress conditions (constant voltage vs constant current; T50 vs T70) and conflicting statements on “no passivation” versus presence of parylene passivation in Methods.
Some key circuit and geometry details for PPG (distance and orientation between PLED and OPD, optical isolation, adhesive optical properties) are missing.
Limited benchmarking against state-of-the-art flexible PPG/oximetry systems (including NIR implementations and low-dark-current OPDs) in terms of SNR, motion robustness, and energy efficiency.
No comparison of system-level power budgets (PLED optical power needed for reliable PPG) versus prior self-powered or battery-powered flexible systems.

PNIPAM actuation depends on localized heating above LCST; thermal margins to avoid tissue damage (e.g., safe temperature-time exposure, SAR) are not comprehensively quantified in realistic in vivo conditions and depths.

Long-term stability and biofouling of embedded conductive nanomaterials (AgNWs, MXene) are insufficiently addressed; silver ion leaching risk and chronic encapsulation integrity (2 µm parylene) warrant deeper study.
The output actuation force, speed, and durability under physiologically relevant cyclic loads (10^5–10^7 cycles for cardiac/vascular/bladder) are not characterized longitudinally.

Wireless LC readout at 260–340 MHz and 15 MHz RF power transfer lack detailed in-tissue range, alignment tolerance, and SAR modeling; coupling through multilayer tissue phantoms or large-animal in vivo data would strengthen claims.
Closed-loop bladder stimulation is demonstrated on a bench model; no in vivo urodynamic benchmarks (e.g., voiding efficacy, stimulation thresholds, safety) are provided.
Cardiac pacing experiments report ECG capture but lack systematic pacing thresholds, charge density limits, electrode impedance evolution, and chronic tissue response.
The ingestible robot’s gastric retention, motility safety, and drug release kinetics over clinically relevant timescales (days) are not established beyond short in vitro tests.
Some key quantitative parameters are scattered or missing: layer thicknesses per module, exact sensor geometries, actuation time constants, thermal interface temperatures.
Cross-sensitivity analyses (e.g., strain vs. temperature for RGO/PI, humidity and ionic strength effects on pH sensor and hydrogel capacitors) could be more explicit.

Limited benchmarking against state-of-the-art wireless passive LC implantables and flexible cardiovascular sensors (e.g., recent antenna-integrated capacitive systems) and against bladder monitoring alternatives (wearable ultrasound, bio-impedance) leaves contextual performance unclear.
Comparisons to other soft robotic actuators regarding force density, response speed, and energy efficiency are qualitative; a standardized benchmark table would help.

The study is largely correlative; causal tests that transcriptional activation drives boundary formation or inter-arm compaction (e.g., transcription inhibition/activation, RNAP perturbations) are not presented.

Molecular effectors of chromosome organization (SMC/ParB, Lsr2-like NAPs, HU/HupS) are not interrogated; no ChIP-seq or genetic perturbations are used to connect boundaries/secondary diagonal to specific proteins.
3C-seq normalization and cross-condition comparability (e.g., coverage, ICE/KR normalization) are not fully detailed, making it hard to assess possible technical contributions to boundary loss/gain.

The 3C-seq analysis at differentiation is limited to a single late time point (48 h) and one medium (MP5); a denser time course would better capture remodeling dynamics and rule out batch/media effects.
Boundary detection in lowly transcribed terminal regions during exponential growth may be underpowered; absence of boundaries might reflect limited signal rather than true lack of domain structure.
Antisense-transcription in GC-rich genomes can be affected by library prep and mapping biases; additional controls or orthogonal validation (e.g., GRO-seq, spike-ins) are not provided.
Some key computational definitions (frontier index, dispersion index) would benefit from clearer formalization and reporting of parameter choices and significance thresholds.
The “open” versus “closed” terminology is evocative but could be more quantitatively anchored (e.g., global compaction metrics, polymer-model-informed descriptors).
Little discussion of SMC/ParB-driven arm alignment in bacteria and how these might underpin the observed secondary diagonal and its growth-phase dependence.

No cross-validation with alternative boundary/TAD callers (e.g., statistical change-point methods or spectral multi-resolution clustering) or topology-aware analyses (e.g., persistent homology) to test robustness of boundary calls.
